title: Best Time of Year to Seal Pavers in Arizona
description: Timing is everything when it comes to sealing pavers in Arizona. Here's when professionals schedule jobs — and when to avoid.
excerpt: Timing your paver sealing project matters. Find out which months offer ideal temperature and humidity conditions for a perfect seal in the Phoenix metro area.

children.text: In most parts of the country, you can seal pavers on any dry day without much thought. In Arizona, timing is a genuine technical consideration. The extreme heat, intense UV, and summer monsoon season all affect how a sealer performs — from application through final cure. Choosing the right window can be the difference between a seal that lasts three years and one that bubbles and fails in six months.
Why Timing Matters More in Arizona

Sealers are chemical products that require specific conditions to cure properly. Temperature affects how fast solvents evaporate, how long the sealer remains workable (called "open time"), and how well it bonds to the paver surface. In a moderate climate, these variables stay within acceptable ranges naturally. In Arizona, they don't.

When pavers are 140–160°F on a July afternoon, a solvent-based sealer can flash-dry on contact — meaning the surface skins over before the product has fully penetrated or leveled. The result is streaking, bubbling, or a milky haze that cannot be fixed without stripping and reapplying. Water-based sealers are even more sensitive to heat, losing workability almost immediately on scorching surfaces.
On the other end, if temperatures drop below 50°F — rare in Phoenix but possible on winter nights in the East Valley — sealers can cure improperly, leaving a soft or tacky finish.
The Ideal Window: October Through April
The broad sweet spot for paver sealing in the Phoenix metro runs from mid-October through the end of April. Within that window, some months are better than others.
Fall (October–November) — Best

October and November are the premier months for paver sealing in Arizona. Daytime air temperatures typically range from 65–85°F, paver surface temperatures stay manageable, and humidity is consistently low. Monsoon season has ended, so there's no threat of afternoon thunderstorms ruining a fresh application. Days are still long enough to complete larger jobs in daylight. Most professional paver sealing companies in the Phoenix area book out weeks in advance during October — if fall sealing is on your plan, schedule early.
Winter (December–February) — Very Good

Winter sealing works well in most of the Phoenix metro. Temperatures are mild, UV is lower, and rainfall is rare. The main caution is nighttime lows: on unusual cold snaps (below 45°F), fresh sealer needs protection or a rescheduled job. In practice, most Phoenix winters allow sealing throughout, with only occasional pauses for cold nights. North Scottsdale and East Valley properties at slightly higher elevations should monitor nighttime temps more carefully in January and February.
Spring (March–April) — Good

March and April remain excellent for sealing, though the window is narrowing as temperatures climb. A job completed in March has effectively the same conditions as fall. By mid-April, afternoon temperatures in Phoenix are regularly hitting 95°F+, and early-morning scheduling becomes more important. April is typically the last reliable month for full-day sealing jobs before summer restrictions take over.
Why Summer Sealing Is Risky

From May through September, paver sealing becomes significantly more complicated. Air temperatures above 100°F are common, and paver surface temperatures in direct sun can exceed 150°F by mid-morning. These conditions create several problems:
Flash drying:
Sealer dries too quickly on contact, before it can level or penetrate properly. Streaking and uneven coverage are the visible result.
Bubbling:
Trapped solvents trying to escape through a rapidly skinning surface create bubbles that harden in place.
Adhesion failure:
Improperly cured sealer doesn't bond well, leading to peeling within months rather than years.
Worker safety:
Working on reflective paver surfaces in 110°F heat is a genuine hazard — reputable companies limit summer scheduling for this reason as well.

If summer sealing is truly necessary — perhaps you're listing your home or preparing for an event — the only workable approach is beginning before sunrise and finishing before 8 or 9 a.m., before surface temperatures climb into the danger zone. Even then, results are less predictable than cool-weather applications.
Monsoon Season Caution (July–September)

Arizona's monsoon season adds an additional complication during the summer months. Afternoon and evening thunderstorms can arrive quickly and with little warning. A fresh sealer application needs at least 48 hours of dry weather to cure before rain exposure — ideally 72 hours for full hardening.

Rain on freshly applied sealer can cause whitening, streaking, and surface blushing as water disrupts the curing process. During active monsoon season, even if temperatures were manageable in the morning, there's always risk that an afternoon storm arrives before the sealer has cured. Professionals generally avoid scheduling new jobs during peak monsoon weeks for this reason.
What Professionals Do

At Go Go Gloss, our busiest scheduling periods are October through November and February through April. We book those months quickly because our clients know these are the best windows for long-lasting results. For summer requests, we evaluate each job individually — considering the property's shade coverage, the sealer type specified, and the forecast. Some jobs work in early summer with early morning scheduling; others we recommend postponing until fall for quality reasons.

When a summer job is urgent and unavoidable, we use shade tents or tarps on smaller patio areas to bring surface temperatures down before applying. It adds time and cost but produces significantly better results than applying to a scorching surface.
The bottom line: if you have flexibility on timing, aim for October, November, or March. You'll get the best adhesion, the most consistent cure, and a sealer that performs at its full rated lifespan.

title: Brick Paver Sealing: Complete Guide for Phoenix Homeowners
description: Brick pavers are classic but require specific sealers and prep. Get the complete guide to protecting brick in the Phoenix metro area.
excerpt: Brick pavers need sealing to prevent fading, weed growth, and sand loss. Our step-by-step guide covers prep, application, and long-term care in Arizona's climate.

children.text: Brick pavers bring a classic, timeless look to Phoenix driveways, walkways, and patios. Whether you have traditional clay brick, modern concrete brick pavers, or reclaimed antique brick, each type has specific sealing requirements — and skipping or shortcutting the process in Arizona's harsh environment leads to rapid deterioration. This guide covers everything you need to know about protecting brick pavers in the Phoenix metro.
Types of Brick Pavers Found in Phoenix
Not all brick is the same, and the differences matter significantly when it comes to sealing product selection and technique.
Clay brick pavers:

Traditional fired clay bricks are the classic choice. They're highly porous, absorb moisture and staining agents readily, and the iron oxide pigments that give them their red and brown tones are vulnerable to fading under Arizona's intense UV. Older Phoenix neighborhoods frequently have clay brick driveways and walkways that have never been sealed — and they show it.
Concrete brick pavers:

More common in newer builds throughout the Phoenix metro, concrete brick pavers are manufactured to mimic the look of clay brick while offering more consistent sizing and color. They're still porous but somewhat less so than traditional clay. Most new construction in Scottsdale, Chandler, and Gilbert uses concrete brick or concrete pavers rather than clay.
Reclaimed/antique brick:

Some homeowners use reclaimed brick for its character and aged appearance. These bricks have often been weathered and may have residue from previous mortar, paint, or sealers. They require a gentle approach — both in cleaning and sealing — to preserve their character without causing damage.
Why Brick Needs Sealing in Arizona
Brick's natural porosity makes it particularly vulnerable to the specific conditions Phoenix homeowners deal with:
Stain absorption:

Unsealed brick acts like a sponge for oil drips from vehicles, rust from metal furniture or equipment, and organic staining from leaves and landscaping. Once absorbed into porous brick, many stains are impossible to remove without aggressive chemical treatment that can damage the brick itself.
UV color fading:

The iron oxide that creates brick's characteristic red and warm brown tones breaks down under sustained UV exposure. Phoenix averages over 300 sunny days per year with UV index values among the highest in the country. Unsealed clay brick can fade noticeably within 2–3 years, losing the rich color that made it attractive in the first place.
Joint sand loss in monsoon season:

Arizona's summer monsoon storms deliver intense, short rainfall events — sometimes an inch of rain in under an hour. This kind of downpour washes joint sand out of unsealed brick installations quickly. Without joint sand, pavers shift, weeds establish in the gaps, and the structural integrity of the installation deteriorates.
Efflorescence:

White or gray salt deposits (efflorescence) are extremely common on Phoenix-area brick due to the Valley's notoriously hard water and alkaline soil. These mineral salts migrate through the brick as water evaporates, leaving chalky deposits on the surface. Left untreated and then sealed over, efflorescence becomes permanently locked in.
Treating Efflorescence Before Sealing

This step is non-negotiable for Phoenix brick sealing jobs. Efflorescence must be fully removed before any sealer is applied — sealing over it locks the mineral deposits in place permanently and often causes the sealer to fail in those areas within months.
Effective efflorescence removal:
Dry brush first:
Use a stiff bristle brush to remove loose surface deposits. Some light efflorescence will come off with brushing alone.
Apply efflorescence cleaner or diluted muriatic acid:

For stubborn deposits, a diluted muriatic acid solution (typically 10:1 water to acid) or a dedicated efflorescence cleaner applied to a wet surface will dissolve the mineral salts. Let it dwell for 5–10 minutes — you'll see fizzing as the acid reacts with the alkaline deposits.
Scrub and rinse thoroughly:
Scrub with a stiff brush and rinse with large amounts of water. Acid treatments must be neutralized completely before sealing — residual acid will compromise sealer adhesion.
Neutralize:
Apply a baking soda and water solution to neutralize any remaining acid, then rinse again.
Allow complete drying:
Brick must be fully dry before sealing — 48–72 hours in Arizona summer heat, potentially longer in cooler months. Even slightly damp brick will cause adhesion problems and sealer whitening.
Best Sealer Types for Brick
Brick sealer selection depends on the type of brick and the desired aesthetic outcome:
Penetrating/impregnating sealers:

The best choice for preservation-focused applications. They protect against moisture and staining without changing the brick's appearance. Ideal for clay brick where natural appearance should be maintained, and for any application where slip resistance is a concern.
Film-forming sealers for color enhancement:

Acrylic or polyurethane film-forming sealers can deepen and enrich the color of darker concrete brick pavers significantly, producing the "wet look" that many homeowners prefer on driveways and front entries. Work well on concrete brick; use cautiously on clay brick.
Avoid high-gloss on authentic clay brick:

High-gloss wet look products on traditional clay brick look unnatural — the plastic-like sheen clashes with the organic, rustic character of the material. If enhancement is desired, a semi-gloss or satin product produces more realistic results. Most professionals recommend matte or low-sheen options for clay.
How to Prepare Brick Pavers for Sealing
Preparation is the most time-consuming part of a quality brick sealing job, and it's where shortcuts have the biggest negative impact on results.
Power wash at 2,500–3,000 PSI:

Brick is softer than concrete and requires lower pressure than a concrete paver cleaning — excessive pressure can erode the brick surface and blow out joint sand. Use a wide-angle tip (25–40 degrees) rather than a pinpoint nozzle.
Treat efflorescence
as described above if present.
Allow complete drying:
48–72 hours minimum in Arizona summer; longer in cooler or humid weather. This is the step most often rushed, and rushed drying is among the top causes of sealer failure.
Re-sand joints with polymeric sand:

Inspect the joints and top off or replace joint sand with polymeric sand. Polymeric sand activates with water to form a semi-rigid bond that resists washing out and resists weed germination significantly better than regular jointing sand. This step, combined with sealing, dramatically extends the time before weed intrusion becomes an issue.
Activate and cure polymeric sand:
After re-sanding, lightly mist the surface to activate the polymer binders. Allow the sand to cure per manufacturer instructions — typically 24 hours — before applying sealer.
How Often to Seal Brick in Phoenix
Resealing frequency depends on the brick type, sealer used, and how heavily the area is used:
Clay brick pavers:

Every 2–3 years in Phoenix. Clay's high porosity means sealer depletes faster than on less porous surfaces. High-traffic areas like driveways may need attention at the 2-year mark; lightly used walkways may go 3 years.
Concrete brick pavers:

Every 3 years for most applications. Concrete brick is more consistent in density and slightly less porous than clay, so sealer lasts longer. Film-forming sealers on concrete brick may show surface wear sooner than penetrating sealers and should be inspected annually.

As with all paver types, the water bead test is your most reliable guide: apply a small amount of water to the surface. Beading means protection is intact. Rapid absorption means it's time to reseal. Scheduling resealing before the sealer fully fails — rather than waiting until the pavers are completely bare — produces better adhesion and a more durable result.

title: Commercial Epoxy Flooring: Benefits for Arizona Businesses
description: Commercial epoxy floors handle forklifts, chemicals, and heavy machinery. Here's what makes epoxy the go-to floor coating for Arizona businesses.
excerpt: Commercial epoxy floors handle heavy foot traffic, forklifts, and chemical spills. Discover how businesses across Metro Phoenix benefit from professional epoxy coatings.

children.text: Walk into a well-maintained warehouse, auto dealership, restaurant kitchen, or medical facility in the Phoenix area and there's a good chance the floor is epoxy-coated. Commercial epoxy flooring has become the standard choice for businesses that need a floor that performs reliably under demanding conditions — not just one that looks good on opening day.
Here's a practical look at what commercial epoxy offers, which industries benefit most, and what to expect from a commercial installation in Arizona.
Why Businesses Choose Epoxy

Commercial environments are hard on floors. Forklifts, heavy equipment, foot traffic in the thousands per day, chemical spills, and frequent cleaning cycles create conditions that destroy standard concrete sealer in months. Epoxy is chosen for commercial applications because it addresses each of these challenges simultaneously:
Durability under traffic:

A properly installed commercial epoxy system handles vehicle and foot traffic without delaminating, chipping, or wearing through. The thick film of 100% solids epoxy distributes load across the concrete rather than concentrating stress at the surface.
Chemical resistance:

Epoxy resists a wide range of commercial chemicals — motor oil, hydraulic fluid, cleaning solvents, food-safe sanitizers, and acidic cleaning agents. Spills sit on the surface rather than penetrating into the concrete, making cleanup fast and preventing long-term staining or substrate damage.
Easy to clean:

Unlike bare concrete (porous, holds stains, difficult to sanitize) or tile (grout lines trap bacteria and debris), a seamless epoxy floor has no joints, cracks, or pores where contamination can hide. It can be mopped, pressure washed, or scrubbed without concern for water infiltration or grout damage.
Professional appearance:

A clean, uniformly coated floor makes a commercial space look maintained and professional. For client-facing spaces — showrooms, reception areas, medical offices — it signals quality. For inspected facilities (food service, pharmaceutical, medical), it also signals compliance.
Slip resistance:
Anti-slip broadcast additives can be incorporated into the topcoat to achieve the wet coefficient of friction required by OSHA and local codes for commercial settings.
Industries That Rely on Commercial Epoxy

Commercial epoxy is not a one-size-fits-all product — different industries need different system specifications — but the following categories represent the most common commercial applications in the Phoenix metro area:
Warehouses and distribution centers:

High-traffic forklift environments need a thick, high-build system that handles point loads from pneumatic tires. Slip-resistant additives are standard, and floor markings (safety lanes, pedestrian paths, loading zones) are often integrated into the coating system.
Auto shops and dealerships:

Automotive environments need chemical resistance to motor oil, brake fluid, antifreeze, and transmission fluid. Decorative flake finishes are popular in dealership service bays and showroom floors for both aesthetics and oil-hiding practicality.
Restaurants and commercial kitchens:

Food service floors require NSF-approved systems, chemical resistance to cleaning agents and food acids, and anti-slip surfaces that comply with health department standards. Coved base (the epoxy "cove" running up the base of walls) is often specified for full sanitary compliance.
Medical and dental facilities:

Healthcare floors need to be antimicrobial, seamless, and easy to disinfect. Light colors are typically specified for visibility of contamination. Specialized antimicrobial additives are available for high-risk clinical environments.
Retail showrooms:

High-end retail and specialty showrooms use epoxy — particularly metallic and decorative systems — to create an environment that reflects their brand positioning. The floor becomes part of the design rather than just the surface people walk on.
Manufacturing floors:

Industrial environments with heavy machinery, chemical processes, or electronics manufacturing (which may require static-dissipative or conductive floor systems) have specific technical requirements that commercial epoxy systems are designed to meet.
Commercial vs. Residential Epoxy — The Differences
Commercial epoxy systems are specified differently from residential garage floor systems in several important ways:
Higher solids content:

Commercial systems typically use 100% solids industrial-grade epoxy with higher film build per coat. Residential systems may use 80–100% solids. The difference matters for durability under heavy traffic.
Thicker overall system:

A three-coat system (primer + base coat + topcoat) is the standard minimum for commercial applications. High-wear environments may specify additional intermediate coats or self-leveling systems that build significant film thickness in a single application.
Faster return to service:

Commercial installations typically use polyurea topcoats that cure rapidly — 4–6 hours to foot traffic, 24 hours for vehicle traffic. This minimizes business downtime compared to waiting 72 hours for a standard epoxy topcoat to cure.
Specialized additives:

Anti-static or conductive additives (for electronics manufacturing), antimicrobial additives (for healthcare and food service), and heavy-duty anti-slip broadcast (aluminum oxide for high-traction applications) are commercial specifications that residential systems rarely need.
Floor marking:

Many commercial installations include painted or taped safety markings — pedestrian paths, forklift lanes, hazard zones — integrated into or applied over the epoxy system. These are subject to OSHA and local code requirements and must be maintained with the floor coating.
OSHA Slip Resistance

Slip-and-fall incidents are one of the leading causes of workplace injuries and liability claims. OSHA and most state and local codes require commercial floors to maintain a wet coefficient of friction (COF) of 0.5 or higher in areas subject to wet conditions.

Standard epoxy and polyaspartic topcoats are moderately slip-resistant when dry but can become slippery when wet. For commercial kitchens, restrooms, loading docks, and other wet-exposure areas, anti-slip broadcast additives are specified:
Aluminum oxide:
A hard, angular mineral that creates aggressive texture. Used in high-traction applications like commercial kitchens, loading docks, and industrial areas.
Shark Grip or silica sand:
Finer texture options for moderate slip resistance in areas that need traction without aggressive texture underfoot — retail floors, medical offices.
At Go Go Gloss, commercial installations include COF testing documentation upon request, providing the compliance records businesses need for inspections and liability purposes.
Installation Around Business Operations

One of the practical concerns for business owners is how to manage a floor installation without shutting down operations. Commercial epoxy installation requires the floor area to be clear and inaccessible during application and initial cure — but there are strategies that minimize disruption:
Off-hours installation:

Scheduling installation overnight and on weekends allows businesses to resume normal operations the following business day. Most commercial floors reach foot-traffic readiness within 4–8 hours of topcoat application with polyurea systems.
Phased installation:

For facilities that cannot fully shut down, the floor is divided into sections. Half the floor is coated while the other half remains in service, then sections are swapped. This approach works well for warehouses, large retail spaces, and restaurants with multiple areas.
Rapid return to service:

With polyurea topcoats, most commercial floors are back in service within 24 hours of the final coat — vehicles included. Full chemical cure typically completes within 7 days, but traffic and cleaning can resume well before that.
Cost for Commercial Epoxy in Arizona
Commercial epoxy pricing in the Phoenix metro area reflects the higher material specifications and more complex installation requirements compared to residential systems:
Standard commercial system
(3-coat, 100% solids epoxy + polyurea topcoat): $3.00–$5.00 per sq ft
High-build or self-leveling systems
(thicker film, specialized additives): $4.00–$7.00 per sq ft
Specialty systems
(conductive, antimicrobial, chemical-resistant topcoats): $5.00–$9.00 per sq ft depending on specification

Volume pricing is available for large commercial spaces. A 10,000 sq ft warehouse floor is priced differently per square foot than a 500 sq ft restaurant kitchen — larger footprints reduce per-square-foot cost due to economies of scale in material and mobilization.

title: Commercial Paver Sealing: Keeping Business Surfaces Professional
description: Commercial paver surfaces face heavy traffic and liability risks. Learn how regular sealing protects your business investment in Arizona.
excerpt: First impressions matter. Discover how commercial paver sealing can protect your investment, reduce liability, and boost curb appeal for Arizona businesses.

children.text: Commercial vs Residential Sealing

Paver sealing at a commercial property is a different undertaking than a residential job in almost every dimension. The square footage is larger — sometimes dramatically so. The traffic is heavier, with dozens or hundreds of people crossing the surface daily instead of one family. Business continuity constraints mean the work often has to happen at night or over a weekend. And the documentation requirements are more rigorous, with most commercial clients needing written scope, material specifications, and proof of insurance before any work begins.

The products are also different. Commercial paver applications warrant sealers with higher solids content — the percentage of actual sealer material that remains on the surface after the carrier evaporates. Higher-solids sealers build a thicker protective film, handle repeated foot and vehicle traffic better, and resist the chemical exposures common to commercial environments. What works fine for a residential patio sealing twice a year would wear out within months under commercial traffic.

Go Go Gloss serves commercial clients across Scottsdale and Metro Phoenix, including retail centers, restaurant groups, hotels, office parks, and medical facilities. Here is what makes commercial paver sealing work in a business context.
High-Traffic Considerations
Commercial paver surfaces are not all the same — and the right sealer for each location depends heavily on what that surface has to endure:
Retail entries and parking areas

need high-durability sealers formulated for vehicle traffic, combined with anti-skid additives. Customer entry points are high foot-traffic zones where a slippery surface creates both safety risk and first-impression problems.
Restaurant patios and outdoor dining areas

require sealers with strong resistance to food oils, grease, acidic beverages, and cleaning chemicals. The staining risk in a restaurant patio environment is substantially higher than a typical residential patio — and pavers that stain are pavers that look dirty to customers.
Hotel pool decks and aquatic areas

have two non-negotiable requirements: anti-slip ratings for wet surfaces, and chemical resistance against pool chlorine, algaecides, and pH-adjustment chemicals that splash and drip onto the surrounding paver surface. Standard residential pool deck sealers are not formulated for this environment.
Office and medical facility entries
typically need a clean, professional finish that holds up to daily traffic while meeting any anti-slip requirements in building codes or ADA standards.
Liability and Slip Prevention

Businesses carry significantly greater liability exposure than homeowners when a slip-and-fall incident occurs on their property. A customer who falls on a slippery sealed surface at a retail center or hotel pool deck has legal recourse against the business, and the cost of that exposure far exceeds the cost of proper sealing with appropriate anti-slip treatment.

The relevant standard for commercial slip resistance is ASTM D2047, which measures the coefficient of friction (COF) of floor surfaces. A wet COF above 0.5 is the general benchmark for pedestrian surfaces — below that, surfaces are considered slip-hazardous in wet conditions. Standard gloss and wet-look sealers applied without anti-slip additives often fall below this threshold when wet, which is why anti-slip additives are not optional on commercial applications.
Go Go Gloss provides:
Anti-slip additives
mixed into the sealer for all pool decks, entry areas, and high-traffic walkways as standard practice on commercial jobs
Certificate of insurance
naming the property owner or manager as additional insured, provided before work begins
Written scope of work
documenting what was applied, where, and when — creating a maintenance record that protects the business if a liability question arises
Scheduling Around Business Operations

The biggest operational challenge in commercial paver sealing is timing. Closing a retail entry or restaurant patio during business hours is not acceptable for most clients — which means the work has to happen when the business is closed or at minimum traffic.
Our commercial scheduling approach:
Night and weekend sealing available

— We schedule crews for evening and overnight starts when needed. Most commercial sealers are dry to foot traffic in 2–4 hours at Arizona temperatures, meaning areas sealed at 9 PM are accessible for morning business hours.
Phased approach for large surfaces
— Rather than closing an entire parking lot or entry complex at once, we seal half the area, allow it to cure, then do the second half. Traffic maintains access to the facility throughout.
Vehicle re-entry timing
— Vehicles should stay off freshly sealed pavers for 24–48 hours depending on temperature and sealer type. We coordinate with property management to arrange temporary parking solutions where needed.
Advance notice to tenants and staff
— For multi-tenant commercial properties, we provide written notice with dates, affected areas, and re-entry times for distribution to tenants.
Written Scope for Management Approval

Most commercial paver sealing jobs require management or ownership approval before work begins — often as part of a formal procurement process or maintenance budget approval. The documentation we provide is structured to support that process:
Itemized quote by zone
— Each distinct area (main entry, parking field, loading area, patio) listed separately with square footage and pricing, so management can approve by zone if needed
Sealer product data sheets
— Technical documentation on the specific sealer product being used, including solids content, slip resistance data, chemical resistance ratings, and recommended maintenance intervals
Certificate of insurance and business license
— Available upon request for any commercial engagement
Timeline and scheduling plan
— Written confirmation of work dates, hours, and phasing to allow property management to coordinate around business operations
Commercial Paver Sealing Pricing
Commercial pricing reflects the scale, product grade, and scheduling requirements of the job. Key factors:
Volume discounts apply
for large commercial jobs — the per-square-foot cost decreases as total area increases
Night and weekend scheduling
carries a modest premium over standard daytime residential rates
Higher-solids commercial sealers
cost more per gallon than standard residential products but cover more area per gallon and last longer under commercial conditions
Maintenance contracts available
for ongoing biennial or annual resealing — contract pricing locks in rates and ensures priority scheduling
