title: DIY vs Professional Paver Sealing: What Arizona Homeowners Get Wrong
description: DIY paver sealing looks simple until you see the results. Here's what professionals do differently — and why it matters in Arizona's heat.
excerpt: Thinking about sealing your own pavers? We break down the pros, cons, costs, and results so you can make the right call for your Scottsdale home.

children.text: Walk into any Home Depot in Scottsdale and you'll find a shelf of paver sealers. The bucket costs $40–$60, the instructions look simple, and the before-and-after photos on the label are convincing. It's natural to wonder whether you really need to hire someone. The honest answer: for small projects and shaded interior spaces, DIY can work. For the driveways, pool decks, and patios that are the staple of Arizona outdoor living, the gap between DIY and professional results is significant — and the cost of getting it wrong can exceed the cost of hiring a professional in the first place.
The DIY Appeal — and the Reality

A professional paver sealing job in Scottsdale typically runs $400–$800 for an average driveway or patio. A bucket of consumer sealer is $50. That math is compelling on the surface. But the comparison ignores several factors: the quality of materials available to consumers, the preparation steps that actually determine how long a seal lasts, and the particular demands that Arizona's climate places on the application process. When we get called in to fix a failed DIY job, the homeowner usually spent $80–$150 on materials and 6–8 hours of their Saturday — and they're still paying us to strip and redo it.
The 3 Things DIYers Almost Always Get Wrong
1. Skipping Proper Preparation

The most common mistake is treating preparation as optional. A quick pass with a garden hose is not preparation. Even a pressure wash — while necessary — is only the first step in a proper prep sequence.

Effective surface preparation for paver sealing includes: pressure washing to remove loose dirt and debris; treating efflorescence (the white salt deposits that are extremely common on Phoenix-area pavers due to hard water); removing or chemically stripping any existing sealer that has degraded or is incompatible with the new product; inspecting and replacing joint sand that has washed out or broken down; and allowing complete drying — which in Arizona means 24–48 hours minimum, not just "looks dry."

Sealing over a surface that hasn't been fully prepared traps dirt, moisture, and old sealer under the new coat. The bond is compromised from day one. Results that should last 2–3 years fail in 6–12 months.
2. Using the Wrong Sealer

Consumer-grade sealers sold at hardware stores are formulated to be affordable and easy to apply. They typically contain 20–35% solids — the active protective components that remain on the surface after solvents evaporate. Commercial-grade sealers used by professional contractors contain 50–70% solids. That's not marketing language; it directly determines the thickness and durability of the protective layer.

Additionally, many consumer sealers are water-based formulas that struggle under Arizona's UV intensity. They're adequate in moderate climates but tend to degrade significantly faster under sustained desert sun. Professionals have access to commercial solvent-based products that aren't available at retail, and they know which products are appropriate for which paver types — a wet-look acrylic that works beautifully on a concrete paver driveway is inappropriate for travertine or a pool deck.
3. Applying Too Thick

The instinct when applying sealer is to put on a generous coat. It seems logical: more product, more protection. In practice, applying sealer too thick is one of the most reliable ways to get a failed result. A thick coat traps solvents below the surface skin, which causes bubbling as they try to escape. It creates an uneven cure where the top hardens while the bottom remains soft. It can produce a milky or cloudy appearance, especially problematic on darker pavers.

Professional application involves two thin coats applied in controlled passes, usually with a pump sprayer and back-rolled with a short-nap roller. The first thin coat penetrates and begins bonding. The second thin coat forms the protective surface layer. This approach produces better adhesion, a more even finish, and significantly longer durability than a single thick coat.
What Can Go Wrong With DIY
The failure modes for DIY paver sealing are consistent enough that experienced contractors can diagnose them on sight:
Bubbling and peeling within 6 months:
Almost always caused by application over an insufficiently dry or prepared surface, or a single thick coat trapping solvents.
Whitening or cloudiness:
Moisture trapped under the sealer film. Common when sealing too soon after pressure washing or when rain arrives before the sealer cures.
Slippery surface on pool deck:
Using a high-gloss film-forming sealer on a pool deck without anti-slip additives. This is a safety hazard, not just an aesthetic problem.
Uneven sheen:
Inconsistent application rate, usually from using a brush or roller without proper technique, or missing sections and doubling back over partially dried areas.
Sealer incompatibility:
Applying a new sealer over an old one that uses a different chemistry. Some combinations cause adhesion failure, discoloration, or chemical reactions that ruin both products.
The 5-Year Cost Comparison
Running the actual numbers often surprises homeowners who assume DIY is always cheaper:
DIY over 5 years:

In Arizona's harsh UV environment, a consumer-grade DIY seal typically lasts 12–18 months before needing attention. At $100–$150 per treatment (materials plus any rented equipment), that's 3–4 treatments over 5 years, totaling $300–$600 in materials alone — plus 6–8 hours of your time per treatment, adding up to 18–32 hours of weekend labor. And that assumes the DIY applications go smoothly, with no failed coats requiring stripping and reapplication.
Professional over 5 years:

A professional job with commercial-grade materials in Arizona typically lasts 2–3 years. At $500–$700 per treatment, that's 2 treatments in 5 years, totaling $1,000–$1,400. The cost is higher, but results are guaranteed, preparation is done correctly, and your weekends are free. The sealer used is also substantially more effective, meaning better protection for your paver investment throughout.

For high-value paver installations — travertine driveways, custom pool decks, large outdoor entertaining spaces — the calculation tilts even further toward professional work. The cost to replace pavers that have been damaged by repeated improper sealing far exceeds any savings from DIY.
When DIY Is Acceptable
We're not categorically against DIY sealing. There are situations where it makes sense:
Small areas under 200 sq ft
that are easy to prep and apply to without specialized equipment
Interior or covered areas
with minimal UV exposure, where consumer-grade water-based sealers perform adequately
When you have prior experience
with the correct commercial products (not the hardware store variety) and proper application technique
Concrete or simple brick pavers
in low-visibility areas where aesthetics matter less than basic protection

If your project involves travertine, any pool deck surface, a front driveway where appearance matters, or an area over 500 square feet, the investment in professional work almost always makes more sense from both a quality and long-term cost perspective.

title: Driveway Paver Sealing: Everything You Need to Know
description: Your driveway takes more abuse than any other paved surface. Here's how to protect it for years with one smart investment.
excerpt: Your driveway bears the heaviest traffic on your property. Find out what makes a driveway sealer different, and how often you should reseal in Arizona's heat.

children.text: Why Driveways Take the Most Abuse

Your paver driveway works harder than any other surface on your property. Every day it bears the weight of vehicles — often 3,000 to 6,000 pounds or more — transferring that load directly to the paver surface. Oil drips, tire scuff marks, and brake fluid spills accumulate over months. And unlike your patio or pool deck, your driveway sits in full sun from morning to afternoon, absorbing maximum UV radiation every single day.

Arizona's climate makes this worse. Pavement surface temperatures in Phoenix regularly exceed 160°F in summer, accelerating the breakdown of both the paver material and any sealer protecting it. Asphalt driveways crack and soften under these conditions — which is a big reason why pavers are the preferred choice in Metro Phoenix. But pavers without sealer are still vulnerable. The sealer is what stands between your investment and years of UV damage, oil saturation, and color loss.
What Driveway Sealing Protects Against
A properly applied sealer forms a protective barrier across the entire paver surface. For driveways specifically, that barrier defends against:
Oil stains

— Motor oil, transmission fluid, and brake fluid can permanently stain unsealed pavers. Once they penetrate the porous surface, they bond with the material and no cleaner will fully remove them. Sealer keeps oil on the surface where it can be wiped away.
Tire scuff marks
— The rubber compounds in tires leave black marks on unsealed pavers. Sealer makes these marks surface-level and removable.
UV fading and color loss
— The most visible form of driveway damage over time. Sealer absorbs UV before it reaches the paver's pigment layer.
Water infiltration and monsoon damage
— Arizona monsoons can dump significant rainfall in short bursts. Unsealed driveways absorb that water, which then migrates to the base, softening the substrate and causing settling.
Chemical spills
— Pool chemicals stored in the garage, fertilizers, and cleaning products can etch or stain unsealed concrete pavers. Sealer provides a chemical-resistant surface layer.
Driveway-Specific Sealer Choices
Not every sealer is right for driveway use. The demands of vehicle traffic and chemical exposure require a more durable product than what works fine on a backyard patio.
Solvent-based sealers

are generally recommended for driveways. They penetrate deeper into the paver, create a stronger bond, and hold up better against oil, chemicals, and the heat cycles driveways experience. They also tend to last longer under vehicle traffic than water-based alternatives.
For finish, most homeowners choose
semi-gloss or wet-look sealers
for their driveways. The enhanced sheen dramatically improves curb appeal — the color looks saturated and rich, and the surface has a finished, intentional look that matte sealers do not provide.
One addition worth discussing with your contractor:
anti-skid additives

for the apron section near the street. This is the entry point where tires transition from asphalt to paver, and where wet surfaces create the most slip risk. A fine aggregate mixed into the sealer provides grip without changing the appearance significantly.
How Long Does Driveway Sealing Last?
Expect 2–3 years from a professional driveway sealing job in Arizona under normal conditions. Several factors shorten that window:
Heavy vehicle use
— Multiple vehicles, trucks, or daily motorcycle parking accelerate wear in the tire path zones
Extreme heat seasons
— Consecutive summers above 115°F break down sealer faster than in milder climates
Chemical exposure
— Frequent oil drips or chemical spills that are not cleaned promptly degrade the sealer surface
Sealer quality
— Commercial-grade sealers with higher solids content outlast box-store products significantly

When the sealer begins to wear, it typically fails first in the tire path — two parallel strips that fade and lose sheen while the rest of the driveway still looks sealed. That is your cue to schedule a reseal before the bare spots allow oil penetration.
The Prep Step That Matters Most for Driveways
Every paver sealing job requires thorough preparation, but driveways have one step that is non-negotiable:
degreasing

Oil stains must be treated with a dedicated degreaser before any washing begins. Here is why this sequence matters: if you pressure wash first, you drive the oil deeper into the paver's pores. The surface looks cleaner, but the oil is now trapped further in. Then when sealer is applied, the sealer bonds on top while the oil stain remains locked underneath — visible as a dark shadow beneath the sealed surface that never goes away.

The correct process is degreaser first, agitation to lift the oil, then pressure washing to remove both the degreaser and the loosened oil together. For driveways with significant oil history, multiple degreaser applications may be needed before the surface is clean enough to seal.
Cost for Driveway Sealing
Driveway sealing costs are based primarily on square footage, plus any additional prep work required. Typical ranges in Metro Phoenix:
Single car driveway
(approximately 300–400 sq ft): $250–$400
Two-car driveway
(approximately 500–700 sq ft): $350–$600
Large or circle driveway

These estimates assume standard prep. Driveways requiring oil degreasing, efflorescence treatment, or joint sand replacement before sealing will have additional costs for those services. A free quote from Go Go Gloss includes a full assessment of prep needs so there are no surprises on job day.

Most homeowners find that sealing their driveway every 2–3 years is far less expensive than replacing pavers damaged by oil penetration or structural failure from unsealed joint sand — paver replacement runs $15–$25 per square foot installed.

title: Epoxy Flooring for Auto Shops and Garages
description: Auto shops need oil-resistant, easy-to-clean floors that look professional. Epoxy is the industry standard — here's why it's the right choice.
excerpt: Auto shops need floors that resist oil, hydraulic fluid, and tire marks while looking sharp. See why epoxy is the standard choice for Arizona's automotive industry.

children.text: Walk into any well-run auto shop and you'll notice the floor. A clean, bright epoxy floor signals professionalism and competence before a customer ever talks to a service advisor. Beyond the impression it makes, epoxy serves a genuine operational purpose in automotive environments — containing chemical spills, improving visibility, and creating a surface that can actually be cleaned properly. Here's what auto shop owners in the Phoenix metro area need to know.
What Auto Shop Floors Deal With
Automotive environments subject floors to a combination of chemical, mechanical, and aesthetic demands that few other commercial spaces match:
Motor oil and transmission fluid spills.

These are routine in any shop doing oil changes, transmission service, or engine work. Both penetrate unsealed concrete permanently, creating stains that can't be removed and creating a slip hazard that compounds over time.
Brake fluid and coolant.

These two fluids are particularly aggressive. Brake fluid (DOT 3, 4, and 5.1) is glycol-based and attacks paint, rubber, and many coating systems on contact. Coolant/antifreeze is slippery and corrosive to concrete substrates. Both require immediate cleanup and a floor system that resists them chemically.
Tire marks and vehicle traffic.

Hot tire pickup — the transfer of plasticizers from warm tires onto a floor coating — is a well-known problem with lower-quality epoxy systems. Vehicle traffic also creates abrasion from tire compounds and debris carried in on treads.
Dropped tools and heavy jack stands.

Impact resistance matters in an auto shop. Dropped wrenches, ratchets, and the legs of floor jacks and jack stands create concentrated impact loads. The floor needs to absorb this without chipping or cracking the coating.
Customer visibility.

A dirty, stained concrete floor doesn't just affect operations — it affects revenue. Customers who walk through your shop evaluate cleanliness as a proxy for quality. A grimy floor suggests careless work habits, even if the mechanical work is excellent.
Chemical Resistance Is Non-Negotiable
Of all the factors in choosing an auto shop floor coating, chemical resistance is the one that determines whether the product lasts or fails within the first few years.
Brake fluid is the key test.

It's one of the most aggressive substances an auto shop floor encounters, and it's one that many lower-cost epoxy systems fail against. DOT brake fluid softens and attacks many coating binders, causing the coating to bubble, delaminate, and eventually fail from the substrate up. If a contractor can't tell you what their product's brake fluid resistance rating is, that's a problem.
Transmission fluid penetrates porous concrete permanently.

Once ATF soaks into bare concrete, it cannot be fully removed. Any coating applied over a transmission fluid-contaminated slab will eventually delaminate at those spots. This is why proper surface preparation — including diamond grinding to remove all contamination — is essential before applying epoxy in any shop that has previously had an uncoated floor.
The right specification: 100% solids epoxy base with polyurea topcoat.

A 100% solids epoxy (not water-based or solvent-based at lower solids content) provides a dense, chemically resistant base layer. A polyurea topcoat over that base provides the highest available resistance to automotive chemicals including brake fluid, coolant, transmission fluid, and petroleum-based products. This combination is the industry standard for serious automotive environments.
Get chemical resistance ratings in writing before signing a contract. Ask specifically about brake fluid (DOT 3 or 4) and coolant resistance.
The Professional Image

The business case for a clean epoxy floor goes beyond operations. In a competitive market like the Phoenix metro area, where customers have no shortage of shop options, first impressions matter more than most shop owners realize.

A clean, bright epoxy floor — particularly in light gray or a gray flake blend — does several things simultaneously. It projects competence and cleanliness to customers walking through. It reflects overhead shop lighting, improving visibility for mechanics working under vehicles. And it photographs well for marketing materials, Google Business Profile photos, and social media — a surprisingly important consideration when customers routinely research shops online before their first visit.
Shops that invest in their floor consistently report that customers comment on it positively. "Your shop is so clean" is a compliment that translates directly into customer confidence and retention.
Slip Safety with Oil Contamination

Oil contamination is the slip-and-fall risk that never fully goes away in an auto shop. Drips from vehicles, splash from oil changes, and residue from fluid spills all create ongoing slip hazards. A smooth epoxy topcoat without any anti-slip broadcast makes this hazard worse — the smooth surface combined with oil creates conditions that dramatically reduce the coefficient of friction.

Aluminum oxide anti-slip broadcast is required for auto shop floors. It's not optional, and any contractor recommending a smooth topcoat for an automotive environment is making a specification error. The broadcast creates a fine texture that maintains traction even when the surface is wet or lightly contaminated with oil.
From a liability standpoint, a slip-and-fall injury in your shop is a serious exposure. Proper anti-slip surface treatment is both a safety necessity and a basic risk management measure.
Drains and Cutouts

Most auto shops have floor drains — sometimes multiple drains in each bay. Working around existing drains requires precision: the epoxy application must terminate cleanly at drain flanges without bridging over the drain opening or creating a raised lip that catches debris or creates a trip hazard.

Professional epoxy contractors who work in auto shops regularly have established techniques for clean drain integration. They cut and mask drain covers during application and ensure the topcoat transitions seamlessly to the drain flange. Ask about drain handling specifically when getting quotes — it's a detail that separates experienced commercial contractors from residential-focused operators.

If you're planning to add a new floor drain in conjunction with your epoxy installation, coordinate that work before the epoxy is applied. Cutting a drain trench through cured epoxy is possible but creates a seam that's harder to finish cleanly than working with fresh concrete.
Installation Timing for Auto Shops
Minimizing downtime is the central concern for any shop owner considering an epoxy installation. The good news: a well-planned project can be completed with very little operational disruption.
Weekend installation.

Most auto shop epoxy projects are scheduled to start Friday evening after the last vehicle leaves, with installation completed over the weekend. Bays are typically ready for vehicle traffic by Monday morning.
Bay-by-bay phased installation.

For shops that operate six or seven days a week and can't close fully, a phased approach installs one or two bays at a time while the others remain operational. This takes longer and costs slightly more to coordinate, but it's a workable solution for high-volume operations.
Back in service in 24 hours.

With a fast-cure polyurea topcoat, a bay coated in the morning can typically accept vehicle traffic by the following morning — 18–24 hours later. This tight turnaround is one of the key advantages of polyurea over traditional epoxy topcoats, which can require 72 hours before vehicle traffic.
Ready to upgrade your shop? Learn more about
our auto shop flooring service
and get a free on-site evaluation.

title: Epoxy Flake vs. Solid Color: Choosing Your Garage Floor Look
description: Flake hides dirt and adds texture. Solid color looks sleek. Both are great options — here's how to choose the right look for your Phoenix garage.
excerpt: Decorative flakes hide imperfections and add texture, while solid color gives a sleek, modern look. Compare both finishes to find your perfect garage floor.

children.text: When homeowners start planning an epoxy garage floor in Phoenix or Scottsdale, one of the first decisions is finish style: decorative flake or solid color? Both are durable, both look great on installation day, and both will serve you well for years. But they have real practical differences that are worth understanding before you choose.
Here's a clear breakdown of each option.
What Epoxy Flake Is

Decorative flake — also called vinyl chip, color flake, or broadcast flake — is the most popular residential garage floor finish in the Phoenix market by a significant margin. In this system, small vinyl color chips are broadcast (scattered) into the wet epoxy base coat immediately after it's spread. The chips embed in the surface, creating a speckled, terrazzo-like pattern.

Once the base coat cures, excess flake is scraped off, and a clear UV-stable polyaspartic topcoat is applied over the entire surface. The result is a floor with visible texture from the chip edges and a multi-tone color pattern.
Practical advantages of epoxy flake:
Hides dirt and debris:
The speckled pattern breaks up the visual field, making dust, tire marks, and light dirt much less visible between cleanings. This is a significant practical advantage for a working garage.
Hides concrete imperfections:
Minor surface variations, old stains, and patched cracks are disguised under the flake pattern in a way that solid color doesn't achieve.
Adds texture:
The chip edges create subtle surface texture that improves traction compared to a perfectly smooth solid-color floor — useful when wet feet or shoes are common.
Versatile aesthetic:
Flake blends come in dozens of color combinations, from neutral gray and beige palettes to bold sports-team colors.
What Solid Color Epoxy Is

Solid color epoxy skips the flake broadcast step. A pigmented base coat is applied to the primed concrete, then topcoated with clear polyaspartic. The result is a smooth, uniform floor in a single color — or in two-tone designs using tape masking to create borders, stripes, or patterns.

Solid color floors have a more modern, minimalist aesthetic. They read as cleaner and more intentional-looking, which appeals to homeowners who want a show garage feel or who are using the space as a gym, studio, or showroom rather than a working garage.
Practical considerations for solid color:
Shows dirt more readily:
Without the visual noise of a flake pattern, dust, tire marks, and debris are more visible. This means more frequent sweeping and mopping to maintain the clean appearance.
Surface imperfections can show through:
Patched cracks and surface variations that flake would hide are more visible under a solid coat. Thorough concrete repair is important before a solid color application.
Sleek, high-end appearance:
For spaces where aesthetics are a priority — show garages, home gyms, commercial showrooms — the clean lines of a solid color floor are often preferred.
Side-by-Side Comparison
Hides dirt between cleanings:
Flake wins clearly.
Sleek, modern appearance:
Solid color wins.
Hides concrete imperfections:
Flake wins.
Shows every speck of dust:
Solid color (which means you clean it more, not that it's worse).
Adds surface texture/traction:
Flake wins.
Best for show garages and display spaces:
Solid color wins.
Most popular choice for residential garages in Phoenix:
Flake, by a wide margin.
Cost difference:
Similar — flake is very slightly higher due to material cost of the chips, but not meaningfully so for most projects.
Popular Flake Color Blends in Phoenix
The decorative flake market has expanded well beyond the basic gray blend, though gray remains the most popular. Here are the most common requests we see from Phoenix and Scottsdale homeowners:
Classic Gray Blend:
The all-time most popular choice — a mix of gray, white, and black chips that complements virtually any garage interior and home exterior. Timeless and low-risk.
Tan/Beige Desert Blend:
Warm neutral tones that complement the natural stone, stucco, and terracotta palettes common in Arizona home design. An excellent choice for homes with desert landscaping.
Charcoal/Black:
A dark, dramatic look popular for show garages and man caves. Shows slightly more dust than gray blends but looks striking with bright lighting and clean vehicles.
Sport Blue or Red:
Bold colors for garage gyms, sports-themed spaces, or car enthusiasts who want the floor to reflect their personality. These stand out — commit to the look before ordering.
Earth Tone Multi:
Blends incorporating rust, brown, tan, and gray chips. Particularly popular in older Scottsdale neighborhoods with warm-toned architectural styles.
How Much Flake Coverage Matters

When specifying a decorative flake floor, the coverage density — how much of the floor surface is covered by chips — is a variable you can control. Coverage levels are typically described as light, medium, or full broadcast:
Light flake (approximately 25% coverage):
The base coat color remains dominant. Chips create accent spots rather than a continuous pattern. The floor reads more like solid color with texture. Less common for residential applications.
Medium flake (approximately 50% coverage):
A balanced, speckled look where both the base color and chips are visible. The most popular density for homeowners who want a visible pattern without full coverage.
Full broadcast (approximately 100% coverage):

The chips completely cover the base coat — no base color is visible through the flake layer. This maximizes dirt-hiding capability and creates the most active, terrazzo-like visual effect. The most popular choice for practical working garages and high-traffic spaces.

Most Go Go Gloss residential installations use a full broadcast, as it delivers the best practical performance for a working garage floor in the Phoenix climate — hiding the inevitable tire dust, Arizona dirt, and daily garage debris that accumulates between cleanings.

If you're still deciding between flake and solid color, our recommendation for most residential garages in the Valley is decorative flake with full broadcast coverage. It looks great, stays looking great with minimal maintenance, and holds up to everyday use for years. If you're building a show space where visual impact matters more than practicality, solid color is worth the trade-off.

title: How to Maintain an Epoxy Floor: Simple Care Guide
description: Epoxy is low-maintenance — but low doesn't mean zero. Here's the simple routine that keeps your epoxy floor looking new for years.
excerpt: Epoxy floors are low-maintenance, but a few simple habits will keep them looking new for years. Learn the do's and don'ts of epoxy floor care in the desert.

children.text: One of the most common questions we get after an epoxy floor installation is: "What do I need to do to keep this looking good?" The honest answer is: not much. Epoxy is one of the lowest-maintenance floor surfaces you can install. But low-maintenance isn't the same as no-maintenance — and knowing the few things that do matter will add years to the life of your floor.
The Good News: Epoxy Is Easy to Maintain

Let's start with what you don't have to do. Epoxy floors do not require waxing, stripping, or specialized cleaning equipment. You don't need to hire a floor care service, rent a floor buffer, or apply seasonal sealers. The maintenance routine for a residential or light-commercial epoxy floor is genuinely simple — and most of it is just basic sweeping and mopping.
The topcoat applied over the base epoxy is the protective layer you're maintaining. Keep that topcoat clean and free from surface damage, and the floor underneath will look great for years.
Weekly Routine
For most residential epoxy floors — garages, laundry rooms, interior spaces — a once-a-week maintenance routine is sufficient.
Dust mop or vacuum to remove grit.

Fine grit and sand particles are the number one cause of surface scratches on epoxy floors. Arizona's environment is particularly relevant here — desert dust and tracked-in sand are everywhere. A dust mop or soft-bristle vacuum attachment removes this grit before it gets ground into the surface underfoot. Don't skip this step and go straight to wet mopping — wet mopping over grit creates a slurry that scratches as you mop.
Damp mop with warm water.

After dry-sweeping, a damp mop with plain warm water removes most of the dirt and residue on a well-maintained epoxy floor. Epoxy's non-porous surface releases dirt easily — you don't need chemicals for routine cleaning.
For stuck-on spots: pH-neutral floor cleaner.

When warm water isn't enough, a pH-neutral floor cleaner diluted in water handles most stuck-on spills and residue. Apply, let it sit for a minute, then mop. Avoid leaving cleaning solutions on the floor for extended periods.
What to Avoid
The things you avoid matter as much as the things you do. Several common cleaning products and habits will degrade your epoxy topcoat over time:
Harsh acids or citrus-based cleaners.

Citric acid and vinegar-based cleaners are popular natural cleaning agents — but they slowly dissolve epoxy topcoats with repeated use. A one-time accidental exposure isn't going to ruin your floor, but regular use will dull and erode the surface over months.
Bleach at full concentration.

Diluted bleach (1:10 or weaker) is generally fine for occasional disinfection on a quality epoxy topcoat. Full-concentration bleach, or repeated exposure to bleach solutions, degrades the topcoat over time. If you need to disinfect, dilute it.
Dragging sharp metal objects.

Tools, metal furniture legs, and equipment with sharp metal bases will scratch the topcoat surface. Use furniture pads under metal legs, and lift rather than drag heavy metal objects across the floor.
High-pH ammonia-based cleaners.
Products like glass cleaner or ammonia-based multi-surface cleaners can streak and dull epoxy finishes with repeated use. Stick to pH-neutral products for regular mopping.
Monthly and Seasonal Maintenance
Beyond the weekly routine, a few periodic tasks keep you ahead of any developing issues:
Check for chips or scratches.

Small topcoat chips and scratches are easy to touch up when caught early. Left unaddressed, they can allow moisture or contaminants to work under the topcoat and expand the damage area. Most professional installers offer touch-up service — or can supply you with a small amount of topcoat material at installation for DIY touch-ups.
Quarterly deep clean.

Every three months or so, do a more thorough clean with a diluted commercial floor cleaner. This removes the light buildup that accumulates even with regular mopping and restores the floor's appearance. In Arizona garage environments — with blowing dust and tire traffic — quarterly deep cleans are particularly worthwhile.
When to Re-Topcoat
Epoxy floors don't last forever without any intervention — but they last a long time, and re-topcoating is far cheaper than full floor replacement.

The topcoat will gradually dull in high-traffic areas over years of use. This is normal wear, not a product failure. The underlying epoxy base remains structurally sound even as the topcoat shows wear. When it's time, a contractor applies a fresh topcoat over the existing floor — no diamond grinding, no new base coat required in most cases.
Signs it's time to re-topcoat:

a dull sheen that no longer responds to cleaning, visible wear paths in traffic areas that don't buff out, or areas where the topcoat has thinned enough that the base coat texture starts to show through.
How long does a topcoat last?

Most residential garage topcoats last 10 or more years with reasonable care. Commercial environments with heavy daily traffic may need re-topcoating every 5–7 years. Either way, re-topcoating is a fraction of the cost of a full new floor installation.
Stain Response
Even with the best maintenance habits, spills happen. The good news: epoxy's non-porous surface gives you time to respond, and most stains clean up completely if addressed promptly.
Act fast.

The single most effective stain-prevention strategy is prompt response. Most substances — including motor oil, paint, food, and chemical spills — wipe right off a clean epoxy surface if cleaned immediately. The longer a substance sits, the higher the chance of temporary staining or surface interaction with the topcoat.
Oil spills.
Blot with a paper towel or absorbent material first to remove the bulk of the oil. Then clean with a pH-neutral degreaser diluted in water. Avoid spreading the oil as you clean.
Rust stains.

Rust stains can appear from metal cans, tools, or hardware left on an epoxy floor — particularly in garage environments. A mild acid cleaner like CLR (Calcium, Lime & Rust remover) addresses rust stains effectively. Always spot-test on an inconspicuous area first, and rinse thoroughly after application.

With these basics in place, your epoxy floor will look great for years with minimal effort. If you have questions about your specific floor or want to schedule a professional inspection, reach out to our team at Go Go Gloss — we're happy to help.

title: Epoxy Garage Floor Coating in Arizona: What You Need to Know
description: Arizona's heat and UV create unique challenges for epoxy garage floors. Here's what works, what doesn't, and what to ask your contractor before hiring.
excerpt: Arizona garages reach extreme temperatures. Learn which epoxy systems hold up to the desert heat and how to get a showroom-quality floor that lasts.

children.text: Epoxy garage floor coatings are one of the most popular home improvements in the Phoenix and Scottsdale area — and for good reason. A properly coated garage floor is durable, easy to clean, and looks great for years. But Arizona presents some installation challenges that homeowners (and contractors) in cooler, cloudier states never have to think about. Get any of them wrong, and you'll be peeling up a failed floor within a couple of years.
Here's what you need to know before hiring an epoxy contractor in the Valley.
Why Arizona Is Different for Epoxy

Most epoxy product instructions and installation guides are written with national averages in mind — moderate temperatures, reasonable humidity, and shade. Arizona is none of those things. The combination of extreme heat, high UV exposure, and desert soil moisture vapor creates a set of conditions that punish contractors who cut corners.
Extreme heat and concrete slab temperatures:

On a summer day in Phoenix, a concrete garage slab sitting in the afternoon sun can reach 140°F or higher. Standard epoxy applied to a hot slab will flash-cure on contact — forming a thin, brittle film rather than a deep chemical bond. The result is delamination: the coating lifts, bubbles, and peels away from the concrete, often within the first season. Even if the slab is shaded inside the garage, radiant heat from the surrounding environment and the concrete itself stays elevated well into the evening.
Moisture vapor transmission:

It sounds counterintuitive, but desert soil does push moisture vapor up through concrete slabs. Arizona's clay-heavy soils retain subsurface moisture, and when the surface heats up, that vapor migrates upward. If there's no vapor barrier primer installed, trapped moisture tries to escape through the epoxy film — causing bubbling and adhesion failure.
UV exposure:

Garages in Arizona are frequently left open, and south- or west-facing garages receive direct sun on the slab and floor coating for hours every day. Standard epoxy resins are not UV-stable — prolonged sun exposure causes the floor to yellow and amber over time, regardless of the original color. A UV-stable topcoat is non-negotiable in Arizona.
The Hot Slab Problem

Epoxy manufacturers specify an application temperature window of roughly 50–90°F for the concrete surface. In Phoenix, that window closes fast. By late spring, concrete slabs are already approaching or exceeding safe application temperatures by mid-morning.
The practical implications for scheduling are significant:
Best installation season:
October through April — this is when slab temps stay in the safe window throughout the day and early evening.
Summer installations:

Possible but require starting before dawn — typically 4–6am — to apply the epoxy before the slab heats up. This requires an experienced crew that has done it before, not a first-timer guessing at timing.
Avoid afternoon summer installations entirely:
If a contractor proposes showing up at noon in July, walk away. No reputable epoxy installer in the Valley works afternoon hours in summer.

Temperature monitoring isn't just about air temperature. A good contractor uses an infrared thermometer to check the actual concrete surface temperature before application — not just the weather forecast.
Moisture Vapor Transmission in Arizona

Before any epoxy is applied, a moisture vapor transmission (MVT) test should be performed on the slab. The two standard methods are a calcium chloride test (placed on the slab for 60–72 hours, then weighed) and an in-situ relative humidity probe test.

Why does this matter in a desert climate? Arizona has significant subsurface moisture in many areas, particularly in older neighborhoods and areas with high clay content in the soil. Irrigation from lawns and landscaping also adds moisture below slabs. When vapor emission rates exceed 3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours, standard epoxy adhesion is compromised.

The solution is a vapor barrier primer — a penetrating primer specifically formulated to block upward moisture migration before the epoxy coats are applied. This adds cost (typically $150–$300), but skipping it on a high-vapor slab means paying for a full reinstallation when the floor fails.
Any professional epoxy contractor in Arizona should offer MVT testing as part of their standard process. If they don't mention it, ask directly.
UV Yellowing on Garage Floors

Standard epoxy resins undergo a chemical process called "ambering" or "yellowing" when exposed to UV light. Even a light gray floor with white flake can develop a distinct yellowish tint after months of sun exposure through an open garage door.

The solution is a UV-stable topcoat. Polyaspartic and polyurea topcoats are UV-resistant and provide excellent protection against yellowing while also delivering superior abrasion resistance compared to standard epoxy topcoats. At Go Go Gloss, every garage floor project includes a UV-stable polyaspartic topcoat as part of our standard system — not as an upsell.

When comparing quotes, ask each contractor specifically what topcoat they use and whether it is UV-stable. If they mention "clear epoxy sealer" as the topcoat, it is not UV-stable. Acceptable answers include polyaspartic, polyurea, or a named UV-stable product with the manufacturer specs.
Diamond Grinding vs. Acid Etching
How the concrete is prepared before epoxy application determines, more than anything else, how long the coating lasts. There are two main approaches: diamond grinding and acid etching.
Diamond grinding

uses a walk-behind machine with diamond-tipped abrasive heads to physically profile the concrete surface. This creates a concrete surface profile (CSP) of 3–4, which is the standard recommended for epoxy adhesion. The grinding also removes laitance (the weak top layer of concrete), surface contamination, and old coatings. It's loud, produces concrete dust, and takes more time — which is why it costs more.
Acid etching

uses muriatic or phosphoric acid to chemically open the concrete pores. It's faster and cheaper, but produces a CSP of only 1–2, which is insufficient for a long-lasting epoxy bond. It also leaves acid residue that must be completely neutralized and rinsed before coating — a step that is frequently rushed or skipped by less experienced crews.

In Arizona's demanding environment, diamond grinding is the professional standard. Any contractor quoting a garage floor coating should be using diamond grinding equipment. Ask directly: "Do you diamond grind, or do you acid etch?" If the answer is acid etch, understand that you are accepting a higher risk of early delamination.
Questions to Ask Your Epoxy Contractor
Before signing a contract with any epoxy floor contractor in the Phoenix area, get clear answers to these questions:
Do you diamond grind?
The answer should be yes, not "we acid etch" or "we use both."
What is your topcoat?
Look for polyaspartic or polyurea. Ask if it is UV-stable.
Do you test for moisture vapor?
They should perform a calcium chloride or RH probe test before applying any product.
What is the solids content of your epoxy?
100% solids is the professional standard; water-based products with 40–60% solids are much thinner and less durable.
What is your warranty?
Reputable contractors offer a labor warranty of at least 2 years. Ask for it in writing.
How do you handle hot slab temperatures?
A good answer: they monitor slab temp with an infrared thermometer and schedule installations accordingly.
Getting the right answers to these questions is the difference between a garage floor that looks great and lasts 15+ years and one that's peeling within a season.

title: Epoxy Floor Coating for Medical Facilities: Clean, Safe & Durable
description: Medical facilities need floors that pass health inspections and hold up to heavy cleaning chemicals. Epoxy delivers both — here's what healthcare facilities need to know.
excerpt: Hospitals and clinics need seamless, hygienic floors that resist bacteria, chemicals, and heavy rolling equipment. See why epoxy is the top choice in healthcare.

children.text: Flooring in a medical facility isn't a cosmetic decision — it's an infection control decision. The wrong floor harbors bacteria, fails health inspections, and deteriorates under the aggressive cleaning protocols that healthcare environments demand. Epoxy coatings have become the go-to solution for clinics, urgent care centers, labs, and hospitals across the country — including here in the Phoenix metro area.
Why Medical Facilities Need Specialized Flooring

Medical environments subject floors to conditions that would destroy most standard commercial flooring within years — sometimes months. The demands are unlike anything found in a typical office or retail space.
Constant exposure to cleaning chemicals.

Healthcare-grade disinfectants — bleach solutions, quaternary ammonium compounds (quats), hydrogen peroxide-based products — are applied daily, often multiple times per shift. Standard vinyl and tile flooring degrades under this chemical load.
Blood, biohazard, and fluid spills.
These are routine in clinical settings and require immediate, thorough cleaning. Any flooring with grout lines, seams, or surface porosity creates a contamination risk.
Heavy wheeled equipment.

IV poles, gurneys, wheelchairs, crash carts, and mobile imaging equipment roll across the floor constantly. Point-load stress from casters damages softer flooring and creates trip hazards at seams and edges.
State health department inspection requirements.

Arizona health department regulations require smooth, non-porous, easily cleanable surfaces in patient care and food preparation areas. Flooring that fails inspection can trigger facility closures or require expensive remediation under deadline pressure.
What Makes Epoxy Ideal for Medical Spaces
Epoxy addresses each of these challenges in a way that few other flooring materials can match at a comparable price point.
Seamless surface with no grout lines.

This is the single most important feature for healthcare flooring. Bacteria, mold, and pathogens colonize grout lines and seams — areas that are nearly impossible to fully disinfect. A properly applied epoxy floor is one continuous surface. There is nowhere for contamination to hide.
Chemical resistance to hospital-grade disinfectants.

A quality epoxy system — particularly one finished with a polyurea or polyaspartic topcoat — is engineered to resist the specific chemicals used in healthcare cleaning protocols. The surface doesn't absorb, swell, or degrade under repeated chemical exposure the way vinyl composition tile (VCT) does.
Smooth enough for effective cleaning.

Mopping and scrubbing are far more effective on a smooth, non-porous surface. Cleaning staff can achieve true disinfection — not just surface-level dirt removal — because there's no texture for pathogens to anchor in.
Antimicrobial additive compatibility.

Modern epoxy systems can incorporate silver ion antimicrobial additives directly into the topcoat formulation. These additives actively inhibit bacterial growth on the floor surface between cleanings — an increasingly important feature in high-acuity healthcare environments.
Chemical Resistance Requirements

Not all epoxy systems offer the same level of chemical resistance. When specifying or purchasing epoxy for a medical facility, the following requirements should be confirmed in writing with your contractor:
Isopropyl alcohol (70%).
IPA is used extensively for surface disinfection in medical settings. Your epoxy system must be rated to withstand repeated IPA contact without softening or hazing.
Bleach solutions at cleaning concentrations.

Diluted sodium hypochlorite (bleach) at typical healthcare cleaning concentrations (1:10 to 1:100 dilutions) should not degrade a properly formulated epoxy system with a topcoat. Prolonged full-concentration bleach exposure is a different matter — discuss protocols with your installer.
Polyurea topcoat for best chemical resistance.

Of the available topcoat options, polyurea provides the highest chemical resistance, the most durable surface hardness, and the fastest return to service after installation. For medical facilities, we strongly recommend polyurea over standard polyacrylic or water-based topcoats.
Request chemical resistance documentation.

Ask your installer or flooring contractor to provide the product data sheet (PDS) for the specific topcoat being used. Chemical resistance ratings should be listed by substance — if they're not, ask for them before signing a contract.
Antimicrobial Epoxy Options
The antimicrobial epoxy category has grown significantly as healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) have received more regulatory and insurance scrutiny. Here's how it works in practice:
Silver ion additives

are blended into the topcoat formulation during manufacturing or at the point of application. Silver ions are a well-established antimicrobial agent — they disrupt bacterial cell membranes and interfere with reproduction. When integrated into an epoxy topcoat, they provide continuous inhibition of bacterial growth on the floor surface.

These additives don't replace cleaning protocols — they supplement them. Between mopping cycles, the floor surface actively resists bacterial colonization rather than passively waiting for the next cleaning round. This is particularly valuable in high-traffic corridors, waiting rooms, and patient care areas where contamination reintroduction is constant.

Antimicrobial epoxy is increasingly specified in new construction hospitals and major renovation projects. If your facility is undergoing any expansion or is being built from the ground up, it's worth including antimicrobial topcoat in your flooring specification from the start — retrofitting it later requires full re-topcoating.
Slip Resistance in Medical Settings

Medical facility floors get wet — from mopping, from spills, from patients and staff tracking in rain. Slip-and-fall injuries are among the most common liability exposures for healthcare facilities, and the floor plays a central role in prevention.

The standard reference for slip resistance in healthcare is a coefficient of friction (COF) greater than 0.6 — the threshold recommended by healthcare safety organizations for wet surfaces in patient areas. Standard epoxy, when polished or topcoated smooth, falls below this threshold when wet.

The solution is anti-slip broadcast: fine aluminum oxide particles are broadcast into the topcoat while it's still wet, creating a textured surface that dramatically increases COF without significantly affecting cleanability. The result is a floor that's both slip-resistant and easy to mop. Ask your installer to specify the broadcast rate and provide COF documentation.
Installation Around Patient Care

One of the most common concerns healthcare facility managers raise is disruption to operations. Medical facilities can't simply close for a week while floors are coated. The good news: a well-planned epoxy installation can be completed with minimal disruption.
Off-hours and weekend installation.
Most medical facility epoxy work is scheduled for evening, overnight, and weekend hours when patient volumes are lowest. A single room or corridor can be completed in one overnight shift.
Quick-cure polyurea topcoats.

A polyurea topcoat cures fast enough that a floor coated at midnight can be back in service by 6 AM the next morning. This is one of the main reasons polyurea is preferred over standard epoxy topcoats in healthcare settings.
HVAC isolation during application.

Epoxy and polyurea coatings produce fumes during application that should not circulate through a facility's HVAC system. Professional contractors working in healthcare settings will coordinate with facilities management to isolate HVAC zones during application and maintain adequate ventilation.

title: Epoxy Floors for New Construction: Start Right
description: New construction is the ideal time to install epoxy floors — the slab is fresh, conditions are controlled, and you avoid the cost of stripping old coatings.
excerpt: New construction is the perfect time to install epoxy floors — concrete is fresh, prep is minimal, and you can choose your finish from scratch. Here's what to know.

children.text: If you're building a new home, adding a shop, or constructing a commercial space in the Phoenix metro area, you have a window of opportunity that retrofit projects never get: a clean slate. Fresh concrete with no stains, no old sealers, no previous coating failures, and no contamination from years of use. New construction is the ideal time to install epoxy floors — and with the right planning, it's also the easiest and most cost-effective time to do it.
Why New Construction Is the Best Time for Epoxy
Homeowners and builders who defer the epoxy decision often end up paying more later. Here's what makes new construction the preferred scenario for any epoxy installer:
No existing coatings to strip.

Stripping old paint, sealers, or failed coatings from a concrete slab requires additional labor, equipment, and time. In new construction, that work simply doesn't exist. The diamond grinder goes directly to bare, clean concrete.
The slab is in its best possible condition.

No oil stains from years of vehicle use, no rust rings from cans and equipment, no penetrating contamination that requires deep grinding to remove. A fresh slab is as close to ideal substrate conditions as you'll ever have.
Concrete mix and finish can be specified for epoxy.

If you're involved in the design phase of a new building, you can specify concrete mix, finishing method, and surface texture that optimizes for epoxy adhesion. This is an option that simply doesn't exist on an existing slab.
Construction sequencing can be planned around the floor.

On a retrofit project, the floor has to work around everything else. In new construction, the epoxy installation can be sequenced properly within the construction schedule — after the slab is clean and other trades are done, before final occupancy.
Concrete Cure Time Requirement

The most important new construction scheduling consideration is concrete cure time. This is non-negotiable: concrete must be allowed to cure adequately before epoxy is applied, or the installation will fail.
Minimum 28 days of cure time.

Concrete reaches approximately 80% of its design strength at 28 days under normal curing conditions. Epoxy applied before this point is bonding to concrete that is still off-gassing moisture — a primary cause of epoxy delamination.
Moisture content below 4 lbs/1,000 sq ft/24 hrs.

This is the standard moisture vapor emission rate (MVER) threshold for epoxy applications. Your epoxy contractor should test the slab moisture before application using a calcium chloride test or an in-situ relative humidity probe. Arizona's dry climate is generally helpful here, but a fresh slab is still actively drying internally even when the surface feels dry.
Don't let other trades contaminate the slab.

Construction sites are busy environments. Once the slab is poured and curing, protect it from oil drips from equipment, concrete sealer applications by other trades, paint overspray, and drywall compound or stucco splatter. Any of these contaminate the surface and require additional preparation before epoxy can be applied.
Mark the slab in the construction schedule.

Put "HOLD FOR EPOXY — DO NOT COAT OR SEAL" in writing on the construction schedule and communicate it to the GC and all subcontractors. Sealers and curing compounds applied to concrete by other trades can prevent epoxy adhesion and may require extensive mechanical removal.
Coordinating with Your General Contractor

Epoxy is a finish trade — it goes near the end of construction, after the messy work is done. Understanding where it fits in the construction sequence prevents both delays and damage to the finished floor.
Trades that must be complete before epoxy:

rough and finish mechanical (HVAC, plumbing), electrical (conduit penetrations through the slab), framing and drywall, painting (avoid overspray on the slab). Any work that generates dust, moisture, or debris should be done and cleaned up before epoxy goes down.
Trades that follow epoxy:

final cleaning, punch list work that doesn't involve the floor, occupancy inspection. Once the epoxy is down, the floor is done — protect it from construction traffic with ram board or similar protection if other trades still need access.
Get a written hold period in the GC schedule.

Verbal agreements in construction are forgotten quickly. A written schedule hold for the epoxy installation — with dates and sequencing documented — protects your installation from being rushed, pushed back, or exposed to contamination from other work happening concurrently.
New Construction Epoxy Specifications
When including epoxy in a new construction scope, the following specifications should be written into the contract — not left to the installer's discretion:
Diamond grind, not acid etch.

Diamond grinding opens the concrete surface profile mechanically, without the chemical variability and neutralization requirements of acid etching. On a new slab, diamond grinding is cleaner, more consistent, and produces better adhesion. If a contractor proposes acid etching as the only surface prep method, ask why.
100% solids epoxy base, not water-based.

Water-based epoxy products are easier to apply and have lower VOC, but they don't deliver the same film build, chemical resistance, or adhesion of a 100% solids system. Specify 100% solids in the contract.
UV-stable topcoat: polyaspartic or polyurea.

For any space with UV exposure — including Arizona garages where sunlight reaches the floor through open doors — a UV-stable aliphatic topcoat prevents yellowing. Specify polyaspartic or aliphatic polyurea, not aromatic formulations.
COF test results from the installer.

Ask for documented coefficient of friction test results, particularly for any floor that will be used by people (not just vehicle-only areas). This confirms the anti-slip broadcast was applied at the specified rate and the floor meets safety requirements.
Popular New Construction Finish Choices
With a fresh slab and no constraints from existing conditions, new construction gives you the full range of epoxy finish options. Here are the most popular choices by application type:
Garage:
Full-broadcast flake in classic gray or tan blend. Practical, durable, hides tire marks and dirt, and has strong resale appeal. The most popular residential choice in the Phoenix market.
Gym or fitness space:
Rubber chip broadcast or a solid dark color (charcoal, black). Provides a performance aesthetic and adequate slip resistance for athletic use.
Showroom or display space:
Metallic epoxy or high-gloss solid color. Creates a premium visual environment. Best in spaces with controlled climate and foot traffic that doesn't include heavy equipment.
Commercial warehouse or industrial:
Solid industrial color with anti-slip broadcast. Prioritizes durability, chemical resistance, and floor marking compatibility over decorative finish.
