title: Restaurant Epoxy Floors: Durable, Safe & Easy to Clean
description: Restaurant kitchens are the hardest floors on earth to maintain. Here's why epoxy is the industry standard for commercial food service environments.
excerpt: Restaurant floors take grease, moisture, and constant foot traffic. Epoxy coatings with anti-slip additives meet health code requirements and are easy to clean.

children.text: If you've ever managed a commercial kitchen, you know the floor takes punishment that would destroy most residential or light-commercial flooring inside a year. Grease, heat, constant foot traffic, high-pressure cleaning, and health inspector scrutiny make the restaurant kitchen floor one of the most demanding surfaces in any built environment. Epoxy has become the industry standard for good reason — here's why it outperforms the alternatives.
What Restaurant Floors Have to Survive
Before choosing any flooring product for a food service environment, it helps to be honest about what the floor will actually face every day:
Grease, food spills, and constant foot traffic.
A busy kitchen generates grease mist, food splatter, and liquid spills continuously throughout every service. Staff are on their feet all day, walking through it repeatedly.
Heavy kitchen equipment.

Commercial ranges, fryers, refrigeration units, and prep tables all rest on the floor. Some equipment is on casters and rolled frequently — creating concentrated point loads and abrasion at caster contact points.
High-pressure hot water cleaning.

End-of-day kitchen cleaning typically involves hot water, high-pressure hoses, and strong degreasers. The floor has to withstand this daily without the coating delaminating, the surface pitting, or the substrate absorbing water.
Health department inspections.

Arizona county health departments require food preparation areas to have smooth, non-porous, and easily cleanable floor surfaces. Failing this requirement can result in failed inspections, fines, and forced closures.
Grease Resistance

Grease is the defining challenge of any commercial kitchen floor. Animal fat from proteins, cooking oils used in sautéing, and fry grease from deep fryers all end up on the floor surface daily — sometimes in significant quantities.

Standard flooring materials absorb grease over time. Porous tile absorbs it through the surface and into the substrate. Grout lines trap it permanently. Even sealed concrete eventually develops grease staining in high-spill zones near fryers and prep stations. The results are a slip hazard, a failed health inspection, and a floor that looks perpetually dirty no matter how often it's cleaned.

Epoxy's seamless, non-porous surface prevents grease from penetrating. Grease stays on the surface where it can be wiped, mopped, and removed. There's no grout to stain, no substrate to absorb contamination.
Important caveat:

epoxy is slippery when wet with grease if no anti-slip broadcast is applied. In restaurant kitchens, anti-slip broadcast (typically aluminum oxide) is not optional — it's required for safety. Any contractor quoting kitchen epoxy without including anti-slip broadcast in the spec is cutting corners. Make sure it's in the quote.
Health Code Requirements

Most Arizona county health codes (Maricopa County included) require that floors in food preparation and storage areas be smooth, non-absorbent, easily cleanable, and in good repair. The specific language varies by jurisdiction, but the requirements consistently point toward epoxy as the compliant solution:
Smooth surface — epoxy with topcoat satisfies this requirement
Non-porous — 100% solids epoxy has essentially zero porosity
Easily cleanable — seamless surface with no grout lines
Good repair — epoxy with a quality topcoat remains in good repair for years with proper maintenance

A reputable epoxy flooring contractor should be able to provide documentation of the floor system's compliance for use during health inspections. Ask for the product data sheet and any applicable NSF certifications at the time of installation.
Front of House vs Back of House
Restaurants have two distinct flooring environments with different priorities, and a good epoxy contractor can handle both.
Kitchen (back of house)

The kitchen needs maximum functionality: high chemical resistance, mandatory anti-slip broadcast, and a surface that can be aggressively cleaned daily. Product specification should include 100% solids epoxy base coat and a polyurea topcoat for best chemical and abrasion resistance. Color is secondary to performance — light gray is popular because it makes cleaning deficiencies visible, which helps maintain standards.
Dining room (front of house)

The dining room has a different audience: guests. Here, the floor is a design element that contributes to the overall experience of the space. Decorative epoxy — including metallic finishes, custom flake blends, or high-gloss solid colors — can create a polished, memorable environment without the heavy-duty spec required in the kitchen. Chemical resistance requirements are lower, so the product spec can emphasize appearance and finish quality.

Having a single contractor handle both spaces ensures product compatibility, consistent installation quality, and simplified project management. It also allows for cost efficiency on materials and mobilization.
Installation Timing for Restaurants
The primary operational concern restaurant owners have about epoxy installation is downtime. In most cases, the answer is: less than you'd expect.
Overnight installation.

A kitchen floor can typically be installed overnight — close after dinner service, install through the night, and reopen for lunch the next day. This is the most common approach for single-room projects.
Full floor return to service in 12–18 hours.

With a polyurea topcoat, a properly installed floor is ready for light foot traffic in 4–6 hours and full service in 12–18 hours. This makes overnight installs completely feasible for most restaurant kitchens.
Phased installation.

For restaurants that cannot close fully, a phased approach — installing half the kitchen one night, the other half the next — allows continuous partial operation. This requires more planning and coordination, but it's a workable solution for high-volume operations.
Cost for Restaurant Epoxy
Epoxy flooring for restaurants is priced differently depending on the environment and specification:
Kitchen (back of house): $4–$7/sq ft.
Higher cost reflects the anti-slip broadcast, chemical-resistance spec, and more rigorous surface preparation required in a contaminated kitchen environment.
Dining room (front of house): $3–$6/sq ft.
Pricing varies based on the decorative finish selected — standard flake is at the lower end, metallic and custom finishes at the upper end.
Maintenance contracts.

Annual or biennial topcoat inspection and touch-up services are available for commercial clients. Staying ahead of topcoat wear is far more cost-effective than waiting for the base coat to be exposed and requiring a full recoat.

title: When and How to Strip Old Paver Sealer
description: Sometimes a fresh seal isn't enough — you need to strip the old one first. Here's how to know when stripping is necessary and what to expect.
excerpt: Old, peeling sealer can trap moisture and ruin the look of your pavers. Learn when stripping is necessary, what products to use, and when to call a pro.

children.text: Why Old Sealer Sometimes Has to Go

Most paver sealing jobs are straightforward: clean the surface, let it dry, apply new sealer. The new coat bonds to the residual old sealer and the paver, extending protection for another 2–3 years. But that process only works when the existing sealer is still in reasonably good condition — adhering firmly to the paver surface and chemically compatible with whatever product is going on top.

When the old sealer has failed, applying new sealer over it does not fix the problem — it magnifies it. The new coat bonds to a surface that is already peeling, hazing, or delaminating. Within months, you have the same failure mode playing out again, now with two layers of bad sealer to deal with instead of one. Stripping becomes the only path to a result that actually lasts.
Signs You Need Stripping (Not Just Resealing)
These are the indicators that tell us a surface needs to be stripped before new sealer goes down:
Peeling or flaking patches

— If the existing sealer is lifting at the edges, bubbling up in sections, or flaking off when walked on, it has delaminated from the paver surface. New sealer cannot bond to a substrate that is already releasing.
White hazing or milky appearance

— This is trapped moisture under the old sealer, a condition called blushing. It happens when sealer was applied over wet pavers, or when moisture entered through cracks in an aging seal. The haze cannot be resolved by applying more sealer — the trapped moisture has to come out, which means the sealer has to come off.
Dark spotting or watermarks visible under the surface

— Dark patches beneath an otherwise intact-looking sealer indicate moisture intrusion or oil contamination that occurred before or during the previous seal job. Sealing over these patches locks the contamination in permanently.
Bubbling after a previous seal job
— Bubbles that appeared shortly after sealing indicate either moisture off-gassing from below or a solvent compatibility issue. Either way, the layer under the bubbles has failed and must be removed.
Incompatible sealer products

— Solvent-based sealers applied over water-based (latex) sealers, or vice versa, will not bond correctly. The solvent in some products actually dissolves water-based sealers, creating a gel layer instead of a bond. If you do not know what was previously applied or suspect a product mismatch, stripping is the safe choice.
Chemical Stripping vs Mechanical Removal
Chemical Stripping — Most Common
Chemical stripping is the standard approach for the vast majority of sealer removal jobs. The process uses a chemical stripper formulated for the type of sealer being removed:
Xylene-based strippers
for solvent-based acrylic sealers — xylene dissolves the acrylic polymer, releasing it from the paver surface
Water-based removers
for latex and water-based sealers — these use different chemistry to break down the polymer without harsh solvents
The process follows a consistent sequence regardless of product:
Apply the stripper liberally to the surface and allow it to dwell for 20–30 minutes — do not let it dry out during this time
Agitate with a stiff-bristle brush to work the dissolved sealer free from the paver surface and out of the texture
Pressure wash thoroughly to remove the dissolved sealer and chemical residue
Assess the result — heavy sealer buildup from multiple prior applications may require a second stripping pass
Chemical stripping is effective in most cases and does not damage the paver surface when done correctly. It is also significantly less expensive than mechanical removal.
Mechanical Removal — For Extreme Cases

When chemical stripping fails to fully remove heavy sealer buildup, or when the sealer has penetrated so deeply that chemical treatment cannot reach it all, mechanical removal becomes necessary. This involves physical abrasion of the paver surface using diamond grinding equipment or shot blasting.

Mechanical removal is thorough — it removes all surface material down to bare paver — but it is more expensive, more disruptive, and requires careful technique to avoid damaging the paver surface texture. It is appropriate for surfaces with many layers of accumulated sealer, failed epoxy-type sealers, or situations where chemical stripping has been attempted and did not achieve adequate removal.
What Happens After Stripping

Freshly stripped pavers look raw. The color appears flat and the surface looks dry — often more worn and aged than expected. This is completely normal. Years of yellowed or tinted sealer have been masking the paver's actual current condition, and stripping reveals what the pavers really look like underneath.
The stripped surface also needs time before new sealer can be applied:
Standard drying time:
24–48 hours in Arizona summer conditions
After heavy stripping or wet conditions:
48–72 hours with moisture meter verification

One benefit that surprises many homeowners: stripping often reveals the original paver color beneath years of yellowed or discolored sealer buildup. The fresh surface looks dramatically better than expected — sometimes nearly as vibrant as installation day — before new sealer even goes on.

Our technicians assess the existing sealer condition during the initial inspection, identify which removal method is appropriate, and handle the entire process from stripping through the final sealer coat. our sealer stripping service

If you are not sure whether your surface needs stripping or a straightforward reseal, that is exactly what our free inspection is for. We will tell you honestly — if a clean-and-reseal will hold, we will say so. If stripping is needed, we will explain why and show you the problem areas in person.
Cost of Stripping
Stripping adds cost to a sealing job, but significantly less than dealing with a failed seal application months later:
Chemical stripping add-on:
$0.25–$0.50 per square foot on top of standard sealing pricing
Mechanical removal:
priced by the job based on surface condition and equipment requirements
Full strip and reseal packages:
bundled pricing available — call for a quote specific to your surface

For surfaces that clearly need stripping, doing it right the first time is always the better financial decision. A strip-and-reseal that lasts 2–3 years costs far less than resealing over a failing surface, watching it fail again in 6 months, and then stripping and resealing anyway.

title: 5 Signs Your Pavers Need to Be Resealed
description: Not sure if it's time to reseal your pavers? These five warning signs tell you it's time before damage gets expensive to fix.
excerpt: Fading color, sand loss, water absorption — your pavers show clear signals when it's time for a fresh coat. Here's what to look for around your Arizona home.

children.text: How to Know It's Time

Most homeowners try to track the last time they had their pavers sealed and reseal on a schedule. That approach works reasonably well, but Arizona's intense UV and heat mean sealer can fail faster than expected — and there is a simpler method than calendar-watching.

Watch for these five signs. If you see any one of them, it is worth getting a free inspection. If you see two or more, it is past time to reseal. Acting at the first sign keeps the job straightforward and affordable. Waiting until full failure often means a costlier strip-and-reseal rather than a simple clean-and-coat.
Sign 1: Fading Color

Your pavers looked rich and vibrant when they were first sealed. Now they look washed out, chalky, or dull. That visual shift is not cosmetic — it is your pavers telling you the UV protection is gone.

Sealer contains UV-absorbing compounds that sacrifice themselves to protect the pigments in the paver beneath. As the sealer degrades under Arizona's extreme UV index, those compounds are used up. Once they are gone, UV hits the paver directly, breaking down iron oxide and other pigments that give the pavers their color.
What to look for:
Compare pavers in a shaded area (under an overhang or near a wall) to those in full sun. If the sun-exposed pavers look noticeably lighter or duller, the sealer has failed in those areas.
Sign 2: Weeds Are Back

A properly sealed surface locks down the polymeric sand in the joints. That sand, when set correctly, creates a hard barrier that prevents weed seeds from taking root. When the sealer fails, the sand surface breaks down — and weeds push right through.

If you had your pavers professionally sealed and the joints were properly filled with polymeric sand, seeing weeds return is a reliable indicator that the seal on the joint sand has failed. The weeds are not a separate problem to treat — they are a symptom of a sealer that has run its course.
What to look for:
Weeds growing directly out of the joints between pavers, especially along the edges where moisture collects.
Sign 3: Water Soaks In (The Drop Test)
This is the most reliable DIY test for sealer condition, and you can do it in under a minute.
Pour a tablespoon of water onto the paver surface and watch what happens:
Water beads up and sits on the surface:
Sealer is working. You are fine.
Water absorbs slowly (30–60 seconds):
Sealer is thinning. Consider scheduling a reseal soon.
Water absorbs in under 30 seconds:
Sealer is effectively gone. Schedule now.

A healthy sealer acts as a hydrophobic barrier. When that barrier is gone, water — and everything dissolved in it, including oil, minerals, and organic material — penetrates the paver surface and begins causing damage from within. In Arizona, that also means monsoon water can saturate the paver base and shift the substrate.
Sign 4: Stains Are Harder to Clean

One of the primary benefits of sealed pavers is stain resistance. Oil from a car drip, food spills on a sealed patio, rust from metal furniture — all of these should wipe up from a properly sealed surface with minimal effort and a standard cleaner.

When the sealer degrades, those same stains begin penetrating the paver material itself. The longer they sit without a protective barrier, the deeper they go — and some stains, particularly oil and rust, become permanent once they have fully saturated an unsealed paver.
What to look for:
Dark spots that will not come out with a standard cleaner, rust marks around furniture legs, or oil stains in the driveway that seem to sink in rather than wipe off.
Sign 5: Sand Is Washing Away

After a heavy monsoon rain, walk your paved area and look at the low points — the edges, the drain areas, the street gutter in front of your driveway. If you see sand deposits washed to those locations, the joint sand in your paver field is no longer locked in.

Joint sand erosion is a structural problem, not just an aesthetic one. The sand provides lateral restraint for the paver system — it keeps individual pavers from shifting under load. When joints hollow out, pavers wobble, edges sink, and the entire surface becomes vulnerable to accelerated damage.
What to look for:
Sandy deposits at the edges or drain areas after rain, visible gaps between pavers, or a hollow sound when walking on certain sections.
What to Do Next

If you noticed one or more of these signs, the next step is a free inspection — not a rushed reseal. The condition of your existing sealer determines whether you need a straightforward clean and reseal, or whether stripping the old sealer first is required.

title: Travertine Sealing 101: Complete Guide for Arizona Homeowners
description: Travertine is the most popular paver surface in Scottsdale — and the most misunderstood. Here's everything you need to know about sealing it properly.
excerpt: Travertine is a popular paving material in Scottsdale homes. Learn why it needs special treatment, which sealers work best, and how often to reseal.

children.text: Travertine is the defining surface of Scottsdale outdoor living. You'll find it on pool decks, patios, driveways, and walkways across the Valley — and for good reason. Its natural texture, warm earth tones, and relatively cool surface temperature make it ideal for Arizona's climate. But travertine is also one of the most misunderstood paver surfaces when it comes to sealing. Use the wrong product or technique and you can ruin the appearance of an expensive installation in one afternoon. This guide covers everything Arizona homeowners need to know.
Why Travertine Is Different From Other Pavers

Unlike manufactured concrete pavers or kiln-fired brick, travertine is a natural limestone formed by mineral springs. Its defining characteristic — and greatest challenge — is porosity. Travertine is full of natural voids, pits, and channels that formed during its creation. This open structure gives it a beautiful, organic appearance, but it also means the stone absorbs moisture, stains, and cleaning chemicals readily.

In Arizona's environment, this porosity creates specific risks. Desert dust and mineral deposits from Phoenix's notoriously hard water can penetrate unsealed travertine and discolor it permanently. Pool chemical splashback — chlorine and muriatic acid — can etch unsealed travertine surfaces. And Arizona's intense UV radiation fades the natural warm tones of unprotected stone over time, leaving it looking bleached and aged.

Proper sealing preserves the stone's natural beauty and prevents these forms of damage. But travertine requires different sealer chemistry than concrete or brick — applying the wrong product produces results that range from disappointing to genuinely damaging.
Types of Travertine Finish — and How They Affect Sealing
The way your travertine was cut and finished determines its porosity level and which sealing approach is appropriate.
Honed

Honed travertine has a smooth, matte surface produced by grinding and polishing. It's the most common finish for Scottsdale patios and pool decks — elegant without being slippery, and relatively easy to clean. Honed travertine is moderately porous and accepts penetrating sealers well. Its natural pits may be filled with grout or color-matched filler, or left open depending on the homeowner's preference.
Tumbled

Tumbled travertine has been processed to produce rough, rounded edges and an antique, weathered appearance. This finish is popular for rustic or Mediterranean-style outdoor spaces. Tumbled travertine is more porous than honed — its open surface texture absorbs sealer faster and requires more product per square foot. It also absorbs UV damage more quickly, meaning more frequent resealing.
Brushed

Brushed travertine falls between honed and tumbled — it has a slightly textured surface achieved by wire brushing, giving it grip without the full roughness of tumbled stone. Porosity is moderate, and sealing requirements are similar to honed travertine.
The Right Sealer for Travertine
This is where most DIY and even some contractor mistakes happen. Travertine requires a
penetrating (impregnating) sealer
— a product that soaks into the stone rather than forming a film on the surface.

Penetrating sealers work by filling the stone's pores with a hydrophobic and oleophobic resin. The stone looks essentially the same as unsealed, but liquids and stains bead on the surface instead of soaking in. The sealer is invisible, breathable, and does not change the stone's natural texture or appearance. This is the correct approach for travertine.
What you should
not
use on travertine:
Film-forming acrylic sealers:

These create a surface coating rather than penetrating the stone. On travertine, this film can peel and flake as the porous stone's natural moisture movement breaks the bond. It can also create a plastic-looking sheen that looks unnatural on natural stone.
High-gloss wet-look sealers:

These are film-forming products that create a shiny, enhanced appearance. On pool deck travertine, they create a dangerous slip hazard. On patios, they look artificial and require stripping to remove when they fail.
Water-based sealers with low solids content:
Consumer-grade water-based products don't penetrate travertine effectively and provide minimal protection in Arizona's UV environment.
Anti-Slip Considerations for Pool Decks

Travertine pool decks require special attention to slip resistance. Travertine is naturally more slip-resistant when dry than smooth concrete, but when wet — which is constantly the case around a pool — any sealer application changes this equation.

Penetrating sealers generally maintain travertine's natural texture and slip resistance better than film-forming products. However, even a penetrating sealer can slightly increase slip risk on wet travertine, particularly on honed surfaces. For pool decks, anti-slip additives — fine silica or polymer particles that create microscopic texture — should be incorporated into any sealer application.

A matte or natural finish is strongly recommended for pool deck travertine. Never apply a high-gloss or wet-look product to a pool deck without anti-slip additives, and even then, a natural-finish penetrating sealer is the safer and more appropriate choice.
How Often to Seal Travertine in Arizona

Travertine requires more frequent sealing than concrete pavers because penetrating sealers, while durable, don't provide the thick protective film of a surface sealer. Arizona's UV intensity accelerates sealer degradation in the pores of the stone.
Honed travertine:
Every 2–3 years. The smoother surface has slightly lower penetrating sealer consumption and UV exposure per unit area.
Tumbled travertine:
Every 1.5–2 years. Higher surface porosity means more sealer exposure and faster depletion. Pool deck tumbled travertine may need attention at the 18-month mark.
The water bead test is your reliable indicator: pour a small amount of water onto the surface. If it beads up, you have protection. If it soaks in within 30 seconds, it's time to reseal.
Filling Travertine Holes Before Sealing

Travertine's natural pits and voids are a characteristic feature of the stone, but they also collect dirt, grime, and algae over time. Whether to fill them before sealing is a personal preference, but there are practical considerations on each side.

Filling the pits (called "grouting" the travertine) gives the surface a more uniform appearance and makes cleaning easier — no recesses for debris to accumulate. For honed travertine in high-use areas, filling is generally recommended. Professionals use color-matched epoxy filler or cementitious grout that blends with the stone's natural tones.

Leaving the pits open preserves travertine's natural, organic character — a look many homeowners prefer, particularly for tumbled stone where the rough, ancient aesthetic is the point. Unsealed pits are harder to keep clean but are entirely natural.
If your travertine has existing grout fill that has cracked or discolored, addressing this before sealing produces much better results. Sealing over cracked filler locks in the problem.
Cost of Travertine Sealing in Scottsdale
Travertine sealing costs more than comparable concrete paver jobs due to the specialty products required and the more careful application technique involved. In the Scottsdale market, expect:
for standard travertine patios and driveways in good condition
for pool decks requiring anti-slip treatment, heavily porous tumbled travertine, or jobs requiring pre-sealing hole filling
Additional $100–$250
for efflorescence treatment if white salt deposits are present (very common in Phoenix-area travertine due to hard water)

For a typical 800 sq ft travertine pool deck and patio combination in Scottsdale, budget $500–$700 for a complete professional job with quality penetrating sealer. That's a reasonable investment to protect a natural stone surface that costs $8–$15 per sq ft to install.

title: Wet Look vs Matte Paver Sealer: Which Is Right for Your Arizona Home?
description: Choosing between wet look and matte paver sealer is a big decision. Here's how to pick the right finish for your specific surface and situation.
excerpt: Not sure whether to go glossy or natural? We compare wet-look and matte paver sealers side by side — appearance, durability, and cost — so you can decide.

children.text: After deciding to seal your pavers, the next question is: what finish? Wet look and matte are the two broad categories homeowners choose between, and they're genuinely different products with different applications, appearances, and trade-offs. Picking the wrong one for your surface type or use case is one of the most common sealing mistakes we see in the Scottsdale market. Here's how to choose correctly.
What Wet Look Sealer Does

Wet look sealers are film-forming products — they create a surface coating on top of the paver rather than penetrating into it. This coating deepens and enriches paver color dramatically, making the surface look like it was just rained on. Colors pop, contrast increases, and the overall effect is visually striking.

The sheen level varies by product: some wet look sealers produce a high-gloss finish similar to waxed floor tile; others create a semi-gloss with more subtle enhancement. The key characteristic of all wet look products is that you can see and feel the coating on the surface.
Wet look sealer works best on:
Concrete pavers
— manufactured pavers with consistent coloring that benefit from enhancement
Brick pavers
— red brick with wet look sealer creates a vivid, saturated appearance that many homeowners love
Front driveways and entries
where curb appeal and visual impact are priorities
Decorative patios
where a polished, finished look is desired

One caution: wet look sealer can look artificial on natural stone if over-applied or if the wrong gloss level is chosen. A heavy high-gloss coat on travertine or sandstone often reads as plastic rather than premium. Semi-gloss wet look products applied conservatively can work on some natural stones, but penetrating sealers are generally the better choice.
What Matte Sealer Does

Matte sealers — often called natural finish or penetrating sealers — work differently at a fundamental level. Rather than forming a film on the surface, they penetrate into the paver's pores and create an invisible barrier against moisture, staining, and UV degradation. The surface looks essentially the same as unsealed, but it's protected.

Matte sealers are the professional's choice for natural stone, pool decks, and any application where a natural appearance is important. They're also the safer option for slip resistance, since no surface film is added to potentially reduce traction.
Matte sealer works best on:
Travertine
— the most common Scottsdale pool deck material, where natural appearance should be preserved
Limestone and sandstone
— natural stones that look wrong with a surface film
Pool decks
— where slip resistance and chemical compatibility matter more than color enhancement
Any area where a natural, understated look is the goal
Side-by-Side Comparison

cells: Shows dust and tire marks more

children.text: Which Surfaces Suit Which Finish
The clearest way to think about this decision is by surface material:
Wet look:
Concrete pavers, brick, colored concrete, tumbled concrete (if enhanced appearance is desired)
Matte:
Travertine, limestone, sandstone, any natural stone, pool decks regardless of material
Either:
Tumbled concrete pavers where the homeowner prefers natural look vs enhanced appearance — this comes down to personal preference and Go Go Gloss recommends samples before deciding
When in doubt, err toward matte. It's easier to upgrade to a wet look finish on a future resealing cycle than to remove a film-forming wet look sealer from natural stone.
Maintenance Differences

Wet look sealers, because they form a surface film, show surface-level dirt differently than matte sealers. Tire marks on a wet look driveway are highly visible against the glossy background. Dust and pollen that settle on a shiny surface catch light in a way they don't on a matte finish. Wet look driveways and patios tend to need more frequent rinsing to look their best.

Matte sealers are more forgiving on day-to-day appearance. Dust and light debris blend into the natural surface texture rather than standing out against a gloss. For homeowners who want their pavers to look great without frequent cleaning, matte is the lower-maintenance choice.

Both finishes are cleaned the same way for deeper maintenance: a garden hose rinse for routine cleaning, or a low-pressure wash with a pH-neutral cleaner for heavier soil. Avoid high-pressure washing on either — it wears the sealer surface over time.
The Bottom Line for Arizona

Go Go Gloss recommends matte/natural finish sealers for the majority of Arizona projects. Our climate's emphasis on outdoor pools, natural stone surfaces, and barefoot comfort makes the penetrating, natural-look approach the right default for most Scottsdale and Phoenix-area homes.

That said, wet look is genuinely the better choice for clients who want maximum color enhancement on a concrete paver driveway or front entry — particularly for newer builds with vivid-colored pavers where enhancing that color is the goal. We carry both product lines and apply whichever is appropriate for the specific surface and the homeowner's aesthetic priorities.
If you're unsure which direction is right for your project, we're happy to apply a test patch during our quote visit so you can see both options on your actual pavers before committing.

title: Why Arizona Pavers Fade Fast (And How to Stop It)
description: Arizona UV is among the most intense in the US. Learn the science behind paver fading and what actually prevents it.
excerpt: UV radiation is brutal in the Sonoran Desert. Understand the science behind paver fading and the sealer technologies that lock in color for years.

children.text: Arizona's UV Problem

Arizona does not just get a lot of sun — it gets some of the most intense ultraviolet radiation anywhere in the United States. During summer months, the UV index in Phoenix regularly hits 10 or 11, which the EPA classifies as extreme. For comparison, the national average UV index is between 3 and 5. On a summer afternoon in Scottsdale, your pavers are absorbing more than twice the UV energy that pavers in Chicago or Seattle experience.

Phoenix gets more than 300 sunny days per year. There is almost no reprieve. While other climates give surfaces a break through overcast winters and shorter days, Arizona pavers are under assault essentially year-round. That sustained exposure is why paver fading here happens so much faster than homeowners who have lived elsewhere expect.
What UV Actually Does to Pavers
UV radiation damages pavers through several distinct mechanisms, all happening simultaneously:
Pigment breakdown in concrete and clay pavers

— The colors in manufactured pavers come from iron oxide and other mineral pigments mixed into the concrete or clay during production. UV radiation breaks down the chemical bonds in these pigments over time. The warm charcoal that looked so rich when installed slowly shifts to a washed-out gray. The deep terracotta fades toward pale salmon. This is not surface-level — the pigment damage extends into the paver material.
Surface desiccation

— UV combined with Arizona's low humidity pulls moisture from the paver surface faster than it can be replenished. The surface becomes chalky and brittle, losing the density that makes pavers resistant to staining and abrasion.
Joint sand degradation

— The polymeric binders in joint sand are also UV-sensitive. Extended UV exposure breaks down the polymer chains, turning firm joint sand back into loose granules that wash away in rain or blow away in wind.
Travertine bleaching

— Natural travertine responds differently to UV than manufactured pavers. Rather than simply fading, it bleaches — the warm honey and beige tones whiten toward a chalky ivory. UV also deepens the surface pitting that is characteristic of travertine, creating micro-pockets that collect dirt and organic material.
Why Some Colors Fade Faster
Not all paver colors fade at the same rate. Understanding which colors are most vulnerable helps homeowners know where to watch closely:
Dark colors fade most visibly

— Charcoal, dark brown, and slate absorb the most UV energy because they absorb more of the light spectrum. They also show the contrast between faded and original color most dramatically. A charcoal paver that has lost its sealer can look nearly gray within two Arizona summers.
Reds and terracotta fade fastest
— The iron oxide pigments responsible for red tones are particularly UV-sensitive. Red pavers in full Arizona sun can show significant color shift within 12–18 months without sealed protection.
Light and natural colors are more stable
— Tan, cream, and buff tones contain less UV-sensitive pigment and show less visible contrast as they fade. They still fade — but the change is less dramatic against their original lighter baseline.

If you have darker-colored pavers or a red/terracotta installation, staying on top of your sealing schedule is especially important. The visual difference between a well-maintained sealed surface and a neglected one is most striking with these colors.
What UV-Resistant Sealers Actually Do
A quality paver sealer does not simply coat the surface — it acts as a sacrificial UV barrier. The chemistry matters here.

Commercial-grade UV-resistant sealers contain UV-absorbing compounds (typically benzotriazoles or hindered amine light stabilizers) that intercept UV radiation before it can reach the paver surface beneath. These compounds absorb the UV energy and dissipate it as heat rather than allowing it to break down the paver's pigments and surface chemistry.
Here is the key insight:
the sealer degrades instead of the paver

. The UV absorbers in the sealer are consumed over time — they are designed to be. As they are used up, the sealer loses its protective capacity. That is why resealing on schedule matters: you are replenishing the sacrificial layer before it is fully exhausted and UV starts hitting the unprotected paver.

For natural stone like travertine, penetrating sealers are generally preferred. Rather than forming a film on the surface, they penetrate into the stone's pores and protect from within while allowing the stone to breathe. This approach maintains the natural appearance while still providing meaningful UV and moisture protection.
The Fading Timeline Without Sealing
Here is a realistic progression for unsealed pavers in Metro Phoenix:
Year 1:
Minimal visible fading. Pavers look close to installation condition. Invisible UV damage is accumulating but not yet apparent.
Years 2–3:
Noticeable color shift, especially in full-sun areas. Dark colors look lighter, reds look more orange or brown. Joint sand begins to loosen.
Years 4–5:

Significant bleaching across the surface. Joint sand crumbling and washing away in rain. Efflorescence appearing on concrete pavers. Staining from dirt and organic material becoming permanent. Pavers begin to feel rough and porous rather than smooth and solid.
Year 6 and beyond:

Structural concern. Loose joint sand means individual pavers are shifting. Water infiltration to the base is accelerating subsidence. At this stage, some pavers may need replacement in addition to resealing.
How to Prevent Paver Fading
The prevention strategy is straightforward — the challenge is staying consistent with it in Arizona's aggressive environment:
Seal with commercial-grade UV-resistant sealer every 2–3 years
— Consumer products from hardware stores contain lower concentrations of UV absorbers and will not hold up in Arizona conditions the way commercial-grade products do
Do not wait until full failure
— Reseal at the first visible signs of fading. A fresh coat applied to a surface that still has some existing sealer bonds better and lasts longer than one applied to bare, weathered pavers
Address joint sand at each sealing
— Replacing or topping off joint sand at the time of resealing adds minimal cost but dramatically extends the life of the installation as a whole
Keep the surface clean
— Organic material (leaves, mulch, algae) traps moisture against the surface and accelerates degradation. Regular sweeping and occasional rinsing between seal cycles extends sealer life

Go Go Gloss uses commercial-grade UV-resistant sealers on every job in Metro Phoenix. Our products are selected specifically for Arizona's extreme UV conditions — not the same general-purpose sealers used by contractors in cooler, cloudier markets.
